Non hoc dicitur, merita excludendo, sed ut insinuetur quod principaliter adscribendum sit gratiæ Dei, qui etiam præmiat ultra condignum. Electi enim per gratiam merentur vitam æternam. Unde tam meritum quam præmium nostrum, primo et maxime dependet atque procedit ex pietate Dei, et gratia ejus quam efficit in nobis. Hæc autem vita æterna est in Christo Jesu Domino nostro, tanquam in objecto et causa effectiva principali, secundum divinam ejus naturam, sicut in Patre et Spiritu Sancto. Tota enim superbenedicta Trinitas, est causa efficiens et objectum vitæ æternæ, id est beatitudinis electorum. Porro in Jesu Christo, id est per eum, datur nobis gratiose vita æterna, quia sicut jam sæpius dixi, omnia dona nobis per Christum hominem conferuntur.
paras.en: Next the Apostle shows that the end of those things, namely of vices, is the death and damnation of the soul. [[6:23|For the wages of sin|Stipendia enim peccati]], that is, the due retribution inflicted for sin, [[6:23|is death|mors]], temporal and eternal. For from original sin came bodily death, as the punishment of that sin. For which reason we read in the book of Wisdom: [[Wis 1:13|For God made not death|Deus mortem non fecit]]; [[Wis 2:24|But by the envy of the devil, death came into the world|invidia autem diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum]]. And for actual mortal sin eternal death is inflicted, which indeed is from God, since it is a just punishment, as it is written: [[Ecclus 11:14|life and death, poverty and riches, are from God|et mala, vita et mors, paupertas et honestas, a Deo sunt]] […]. [[6:23|But the grace of God|Gratia autem Dei]], that is, from grace or by the grace of God, is given to the just as reward [[6:23|life everlasting|vita æterna]]. This is not said to exclude merits, but to suggest that it is to be ascribed principally to the grace of God, who also rewards beyond what is deserved. For the elect merit eternal life through grace. Hence both our merit and our reward depend and proceed first and chiefly from the loving-kindness of God, and the grace which he works in us. And this [[6:23|life everlasting|vita æterna]] is [[6:23|in Christ Jesus our Lord|in Christo Jesu Domino nostro]], as in its object and principal effective cause, according to his divine nature, as in the Father and the Holy Ghost. For the whole superblessed Trinity is the efficient cause and the object of eternal life, that is, of the beatitude of the elect. Further, in Jesus Christ, that is, through him, eternal life is given us graciously, since, as I have often said already, all gifts are conferred on us through Christ the man.

7.title: Expositio capituli septimi: An ignoratis, fratres, etc.?
7.title_en: Explanation of the seventh chapter: Know you not, brethren?
7.note: Some lines are lost in the transcription at the start of v. 8.

paras.t: In capituli hujus exordio probat Apostolus cessationem legis Mosaicæ per exemplum. An ignoratis, fratres, id est o vos, Romani fideles, an nescitis quæ dicam? Et scio quia non ignoratis ea. Scientibus enim legem loquor, id est vobis Romanis in Christum credentibus : qui partim fuistis sub lege Moysis, et estis ex Judaismo christiani effecti, propter quod legem Moysis scitis; partim vero gentiles fuistis, atque sub civili lege vixistis, et ideo legem hanc nescitis. Barbari vero qui legibus non reguntur, nullam harum legum noverunt. An, inquam, nescitis, quia lex Mosaica, et civilis, in homine dominatur, id est, hominem obligat ad observantiam legis, quanto tempore, id est quamdiu, vivit, id est, vigorem ac statum sortitur lex ipsa? Si autem lex perfectior, priorem evacuans, superveniat, cessat lex prima, nec amplius obligat : sicut cessavit lex Moysis, superveniente lege Christi.
paras.en: At the opening of this chapter the Apostle proves by an example that the Mosaic law has ceased. [[7:1|Know you not, brethren|An ignoratis, fratres]], that is, O you faithful Romans, do you not know what I shall say? And I know that you are not ignorant of it. [[7:1|For I speak to them that know the law|Scientibus enim legem loquor]], that is, to you Romans who believe in Christ: some of you were under the law of Moses and have become Christians out of Judaism, and so you know the law of Moses; others were Gentiles and lived under the civil law, and so you do not know this law. But barbarians, who are not ruled by laws, know neither of these laws. Do you not know, I say, [[7:1|that the law|quia lex]], the Mosaic and the civil, [[7:1|hath dominion over a man|in homine dominatur]], that is, binds a man to keep the law, [[7:1|as long as|quanto tempore]], that is, for as long as, [[7:1|it liveth|vivit]], that is, as long as the law itself keeps its force and standing? But if a more perfect law comes in, doing away with the earlier one, the first law ceases and binds no longer: as the law of Moses ceased when the law of Christ came in.

paras.t: Hujus rei exemplum subjungitur. Nam quæ sub viro est mulier, id est femina legitime maritata et viro subjecta, juxta illud, Sub viri potestate eris; vivente viro, alligata est legi viri, quia tenetur ei debitum reddere, nec potest ab eo discedere. Mulier enim potestatem corporis sui non habet, sed vir. Si autem mortuus fuerit vir ejus, liberata est a lege viri, in tantum ut si vir ejus resurgeret, non teneretur eum recipere, nisi ex condecentia quadam, ut dicitur. Igitur vivente viro, vocabitur adultera si fuerit cum alio viro uxorato, vel non uxorato. Si autem mortuus fuerit vir ejus morte naturali, aut certe civili ante copulam, liberata est a lege, id est a jure, viri, ut non sit adultera si fuerit cum alio viro. Potest enim nubere cui placuerit, tantum nubat in Domino.
paras.en: An example of this follows. [[7:2|For the woman that hath an husband|Nam quæ sub viro est mulier]], that is, a woman lawfully married and subject to her husband, according to the words, [[Gen 3:16|thou shalt be under thy husband's power|Sub viri potestate eris]]; [[7:2|whilst her husband liveth is bound to the law|vivente viro, alligata est legi]] of her husband, because she is bound to render him the debt [that is, the marriage debt], and cannot leave him. For [[1 Cor 7:4|The wife hath not power of her own body: but the husband|Mulier enim potestatem corporis sui non habet, sed vir]]. [[7:2|But if her husband be dead, she is loosed from the law of her husband|Si autem mortuus fuerit vir ejus, liberata est a lege viri]]: so much so that if her husband rose again, she would not be bound to take him back, except out of a certain fittingness, as is said. [[7:3|Therefore, whilst her husband liveth, she shall be called an adulteress, if she be with another man|Igitur vivente viro, vocabitur adultera si fuerit cum alio viro]], whether married or unmarried. [[7:3|but if her husband be dead|Si autem mortuus fuerit vir ejus]] by natural death, or indeed by civil death before the marriage was consummated [civil death: entry into religious profession, which dissolves a marriage not yet consummated], [[7:3|she is delivered from the law|liberata est a lege]], that is, from the right, [[7:3|of her husband: so that she is not an adulteress, if she be with another man|viri, ut non sit adultera si fuerit cum alio viro]]. For she may marry whom she pleases, provided she marry [[1 Cor 7:39|only in the Lord|tantum nubat in Domino]].

paras.t: Præterea applicat præinductam similitudinem Apostolus ad propositum de cessatione legis scriptæ. Itaque, fratres mei, et vos mortificati estis legi, id est a debito et vigore Mosaicæ legis soluti, per corpus Christi, id est per ea quæ Verbum Dei fecit, assumpsit et pertulit in corpore Christi, videlicet per Christi incarnationem, per corporis sui in cruce expansionem, vel etiam per incorporationem qua Christo incorporati, unum estis cum ipso effecti; ut sitis vos alterius, scilicet Christi, qui ex mortuis resurrexit, id est, esse vestrum ac vitam ad Christi gloriam ordinetis, nec vobis ipsis, sed ei vivatis, non sequendo desideria propria, sed Christi mandata, nec insistendo privato amori, sed divinæ caritati. Qui si abnegant semetipsos, cordialiter dicunt illud Psalmistæ : Non nobis, Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam. Ut fructificetis Deo, id est, opera virtuosa agatis ad gloriam Dei. Omnis enim arbor, inquit Salvator, quæ non facit fructum bonum, excidetur, et in ignem mittetur; et rursum, Qui autem manet in me, hic fert fructum multum.
paras.en: Next the Apostle applies the comparison he has brought in to his point about the ceasing of the written law. [[7:4|Therefore, my brethren, you also are become dead to the law|Itaque, fratres mei, et vos mortificati estis legi]], that is, set free from the obligation and force of the Mosaic law, [[7:4|by the body of Christ|per corpus Christi]], that is, by what the Word of God did, took on and suffered in the body of Christ: namely by Christ's incarnation, by the stretching out of His body on the cross, or also by the incorporation by which, incorporated into Christ, you have been made one with Him; [[7:4|that you may belong to another|ut sitis vos alterius]], namely to Christ, [[7:4|who is risen again from the dead|qui ex mortuis resurrexit]]: that is, that you may direct your being and your life to Christ's glory, and live not for yourselves but for Him, following not your own desires but Christ's commandments, and giving yourselves not to private love but to divine charity. Those who deny themselves in this way say from the heart the Psalmist's words: [[Ps 113:9|Not to us, O Lord, not to us; but to thy name give glory|Non nobis, Domine, non nobis, sed nomini tuo da gloriam]] [the margin gives this Psalm by the Hebrew numbering (Ps 115:1)]. [[7:4|that we may bring forth fruit to God|Ut fructificetis Deo]] [Denis reads *fructificetis*, "that you may bring forth fruit"], that is, that you may do virtuous works to the glory of God. For [[Matt 7:19|Every tree|Omnis enim arbor]], says the Saviour, [[Matt 7:19|that bringeth not forth good fruit, shall be cut down, and shall be cast into the fire|quæ non facit fructum bonum, excidetur, et in ignem mittetur]]; and again, [[John 15:5|He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same beareth much fruit|Qui autem manet in me, hic fert fructum multum]] [the margin gives John xv, 6; the words are those of v. 5].

paras.t: Insuper manifestat legem jam esse evacuatam, ex consideratione status qui erat sub lege. Quum enim essemus in carne, id est in carnalibus et cærimonialibus operibus legis, seu vitiis carnis, tempore legis antiquæ, passiones peccatorum, id est passiones, seu sensitivæ partis inordinatæ motiones interiores, quæ per legem erant, id est, ex jussione aut prohibitione legis, ex occasione in nobis incitabantur, operabantur in membris nostris, id est, ad opera prava induxerunt membra nostra, ut oculus per res varias fornicaretur, manus alium cæderet, lingua mentiretur, ut fructificarent morti, id est, opera morti congrua, æternaque morte digna patrarent. Nunc autem, scilicet tempore gratiæ, soluti sumus a lege mortis, id est ab obligatione et observatione Mosaicæ legis : quæ nominatur lex mortis, quia ex occasione mortem spiritualem inferebat, augendo culpam ratione transgressionis præcepti, et incitando concupiscentiam ; vel, quia transgressoribus suis temporalem intulit mortem, sicut per Moysen sæpius dicitur : Qui percusserit hominem vel hoc, morte moriatur. In quo legi passi sumus, id est, ad cujus observantiam obligati eramus, usque ad publicationem evangelicæ legis. Nunc vero soluti sumus, ita ut serviamus Deo in novitate spiritus, id est in spirituali renovatione mentis, quemadmodum scriptum est : Renovamini spiritu mentis vestræ ; vel in novitate spiritualis intelligentiæ ; et non in vetustate litteræ, id est observantiis litteralibus seu cærimonialibus veteris Testamenti. Littera enim occidit, spiritus autem vivificat.
paras.en: Further, he shows that the law has now been done away with, from a consideration of the state that existed under the law. [[7:5|For when we were in the flesh|Quum enim essemus in carne]], that is, in the carnal and ceremonial works of the law, or in the vices of the flesh, in the time of the old law, [[7:5|the passions of sins|passiones peccatorum]], that is, the passions, or disordered inward motions of the sensitive part, [[7:5|which were by the law|quæ per legem erant]], that is, which were stirred up in us, taking occasion from the command or prohibition of the law, [[7:5|did work in our members|operabantur in membris nostris]], that is, led our members to wicked works, so that the eye committed fornication through various things, the hand struck another, the tongue lied[[Rom 6:13||]] [the margin reads Rom. vi, 4; the thought is that of Rom 6:13, on yielding one's members to sin], [[7:5|to bring forth fruit unto death|ut fructificarent morti]], that is, that they might do works fitting for death and deserving eternal death. [[7:6|But now|Nunc autem]], namely in the time of grace, [[7:6|we are loosed from the law of death|soluti sumus a lege mortis]], that is, from the obligation and observance of the Mosaic law: which is called the law of death because it brought in spiritual death by occasion, increasing guilt by reason of the transgression of the precept and by stirring up concupiscence; or because it inflicted temporal death on those who transgressed it, as is often said through Moses: [[Ex 21:12|He that striketh a man with a will to kill him, shall be put to death|Qui percusserit hominem vel hoc, morte moriatur]][[Ex 21:15||]][[Ex 21:17||]][[Deut 21:23||]]. [[7:6|wherein we were detained|In quo legi passi sumus]] [so the transcription; the Vulgate has *in qua detinebamur*], that is, to whose observance we were bound until the publishing of the law of the Gospel. But now we are loosed, [[7:6|so that we should serve in newness of spirit|ita ut serviamus Deo in novitate spiritus]], that is, in the spiritual renewal of the mind, as it is written: [[Eph 4:23|be renewed in spirit of your mind|Renovamini spiritu mentis vestræ]]; or in the newness of spiritual understanding; [[7:6|and not in the oldness of the letter|et non in vetustate litteræ]], that is, in the literal or ceremonial observances of the Old Testament. For [[2 Cor 3:6|the letter killeth: but the spirit quickeneth|Littera enim occidit, spiritus autem vivificat]].

paras.t: Quoniam vero veterem legem vocavit legem mortis, ne quis ex hoc erroris occasionem eliciat, ut Manichæi, dicentes legem Moysis datam a dæmone, removet Apostolus talem errorem. Quid ergo dicemus? Si ita est ut dixi, lex peccatum est? id est, an tunc dicendum sit, quod lex sit vitiosa, peccatique causa per se? Absit. Sed peccatum non cognovi nisi per legem : id est, hoc magis tenendum affirmo quod lex sit bona, quoniam ordinatur ad bonum, scilicet ad discernendum inter bonum et malum, inter virtutes et vitia, quatenus mala vitentur, et bona agantur. Ideo ait, Peccatum non cognovi esse peccatum, saltem ita perfecte atque communiter, nisi per legem, id est legis instructionem : nam concupiscentiam carnalem et inordinatam nesciebam esse peccatum, nisi lex diceret : Non concupisces. Loquitur autem Apostolus in persona generis humani, præsertim eorum in quibus ratio naturalis sic obtenebrata fuerat vitiis, ut inter bonum et malum parum aut nihil discernerent. Quorum multi putabant cogitationes non procedentes in actum pravum, et simplicem fornicationem, atque similia quædam, non esse peccata. De quibus Propheta : Væ qui dicitis malum bonum, et bonum malum, ponentes tenebras lucem, et lucem tenebras. His ergo ostendit lex, quid sit culpabile. Nam et ipsi ignorarent concupiscentiam, nisi lex diceret : Non concupiscies. Ad vitandum autem peccatum, requiritur peccati cognitio : ideo lex potius retrahit a peccato, quam sit causa ipsius. Est tamen occasio peccati per accidens, ex parte nostri, qui sicut naturaliter appetimus libertatem, ita communiter inclinamur ad mutuam in veritatem ne nostra libertas videatur arceri.
paras.en: Since he has called the old law the law of death, lest anyone draw from this an occasion of error, like the Manichees, who said that the law of Moses was given by a demon, the Apostle rules out that error. [[7:7|What shall we say, then|Quid ergo dicemus]]? If it is as I have said, [[7:7|Is the law sin|lex peccatum est]]? that is, must it then be said that the law is faulty, and of itself a cause of sin? [[7:7|God forbid|Absit]]! [[7:7|But I do not know sin, but by the law|Sed peccatum non cognovi nisi per legem]]: that is, I affirm that this is rather to be held, that the law is good, since it is ordained to good, namely to distinguishing between good and evil, between virtues and vices, so that evil may be avoided and good done. So he says: I did not know sin to be sin, at least not so perfectly and generally, except by the law, that is, by the law's teaching: [[7:7|For I had not known concupiscence|nam concupiscentiam nesciebam]], carnal and disordered, to be sin, [[7:7|if the law did not say: Thou shalt not covet|nisi lex diceret : Non concupisces]]. The Apostle speaks here in the person of the human race, especially of those in whom natural reason had been so darkened by vices that they distinguished little or nothing between good and evil. Many of them thought that thoughts not going on into a wicked act, and simple fornication, and certain like things, were not sins. Of them the Prophet says: [[Is 5:20|Woe to you that call evil good, and good evil: that put darkness for light, and light for darkness|Væ qui dicitis malum bonum, et bonum malum, ponentes tenebras lucem, et lucem tenebras]]. To these, then, the law showed what is blameworthy. For they too would not have known concupiscence, if the law did not say: [[Ex 20:17|Thou shalt not covet|Non concupiscies]]. Now to avoid sin, knowledge of sin is required: so the law rather draws us back from sin than is its cause. Yet it is an occasion of sin accidentally, on our part, since just as we naturally desire liberty, so we are commonly inclined toward what is forbidden [the transcription reads *ad mutuam in veritatem*, apparently a misreading of *in vetitum*, "toward the forbidden"], lest our liberty seem to be hemmed in.

paras.t: […] mandatum, id est concupiscentia seu fomes peccati, imo et dæmon tentator, occasionem peccandi seu impugnandi accipiens ex mandato legis, quæ concupiscentiam prohibebat. Ex tali enim mandato irritabatur et provocabatur concupiscentia. Dæmon quoque videns homini datam legem, cœpit fortius eum invadere atque tentare. Sicque peccatum operatum est in me, id est, ad operandum induxit me, omnem concupiscentiam lege prohibitam, ita quod concupiscentia mala processit in opus. Sine lege enim, id est lege nondum accepta, vel ejus cognitione adepta, peccatum mortuum erat, id est, fomes peccati non ita viguit, sed erat debilior : quia non tantum excitatus ut postea, nec tantum impugnabatur a dæmone, minus quoque imputabatur a Deo.
paras.en: […] [the start of v. 8 is lost in the transcription] … sin [the transcription reads *mandatum*, "commandment", here], that is, concupiscence or the tinder of sin [*fomes*: the inclination to sin left in us by original sin], and indeed also the demon who tempts, taking the occasion of sinning or of attacking from the commandment of the law, which forbade concupiscence. For by such a commandment concupiscence was irritated and provoked. The demon too, seeing the law given to man, began to assail and tempt him more strongly. And so sin [[7:8|wrought in me|operatum est in me]], that is, led me to work, [[7:8|all manner of concupiscence|omnem concupiscentiam]] forbidden by the law, so that evil concupiscence went on into deed. [[7:8|For without the law|Sine lege enim]], that is, when the law had not yet been received, or knowledge of it gained, [[7:8|sin was dead|peccatum mortuum erat]], that is, the tinder of sin was not so strong, but weaker: because it was not so stirred up as afterwards, nor was there such assault from the demon, and it was also less imputed by God.

paras.t: Ego autem vivebam sine lege aliquando. Scire oportet quod Apostolus loquitur hic in persona hominis communiter. Unde non omnia quæ dicit, ad eosdem referantur. Nunc ergo loquens in persona hominis, qui ad tempus vixit ante legem Mosaicam, et ad tempus ei subjacuit, dicit : Ego autem vivebam vita gratiæ, vel simpliciter, vel respective, id est carendo peccato mortali, vel minus peccando, sine lege scripta, aliquando, id est, antequam data est lex scripta. Tunc enim, ut dictum est, minus viguit fomes. Sed quum venisset mandatum legis, id est, postquam lex data est mihi, peccatum revixit, id est, fomes seu ejus effectus (videlicet culpa) insolescere, rebellare, vigereque cœpit. Ego autem spiritualiter mortuus sum, sub lege peccato reviviscente in me ; et inventum est mihi, id est ad incommodum meum, mandatum legis, quod ordinatum ac datum erat ad vitam gratiæ in præsenti, vitamque gloriæ in futuro, hoc esse ad mortem culpæ in via, atque ad mortem damnationis in gehenna. Cujus ratio atque declaratio subditur. Nam peccatum, id est concupiscentia seu fomes, occasione accepta per mandatum, secundum sensum jam præinductum, seduxit me, id est, rationem meam subvertit, ut potius inhæreret bono commutabili et caduco quam summo et increato, et per illud, id est hanc seductionem illicitumque consensum, occidit me, inducens me ad delectationem mortiferam, seu culpam mortalem, quæ tollit caritatem, in qua animæ vita consistit.
paras.en: [[7:9|And I lived some time without the law|Ego autem vivebam sine lege aliquando]]. It must be known that the Apostle speaks here in the person of man in general. Hence not everything he says is to be referred to the same people. Speaking now, then, in the person of a man who lived for a time before the Mosaic law and for a time was subject to it, he says: [[7:9|And I lived|Ego autem vivebam]] the life of grace, either simply or relatively, that is, by being free of mortal sin, or by sinning less, [[7:9|without the law|sine lege]] written, [[7:9|some time|aliquando]], that is, before the written law was given. For then, as has been said, the tinder was less strong. [[7:9|But when the commandment came|Sed quum venisset mandatum]] of the law, that is, after the law was given to me, [[7:9|sin revived|peccatum revixit]], that is, the tinder, or its effect (namely guilt), began to grow insolent, to rebel and to be strong. [[7:10|And I died|Ego autem spiritualiter mortuus sum]] spiritually, under the law, as sin revived in me; [[7:10|And the commandment that was ordained to life, the same was found to be|et inventum est mihi mandatum]] to me, that is, to my harm, the commandment of the law, [[7:10|that was ordained to life|quod erat ad vitam]], ordained and given for the life of grace in the present and the life of glory in the future, [[7:10|the same was found to be unto death to me|hoc esse ad mortem]]: to the death of guilt on the way, and to the death of damnation in hell. The reason and explanation of this is added. [[7:11|For sin|Nam peccatum]], that is, concupiscence or the tinder, [[7:11|taking occasion by the commandment|occasione accepta per mandatum]], in the sense already given, [[7:11|seduced me|seduxit me]], that is, overturned my reason, so that it clung to changeable and passing good rather than to the highest and uncreated good, [[7:11|and by it|et per illud]], that is, by this seduction and unlawful consent, [[7:11|killed me|occidit]], leading me to deadly delight, or mortal guilt, which takes away charity, in which the life of the soul consists.

paras.t: Præterea ex prædictis infert Apostolus : Itaque lex quidem scripta, est sancta, quia prohibet vitia, præcipitque honesta. Unde secundum Isidorum : Lex est jussio sancta, jubens honesta. Et mandatum legis, est sanctum, id est ad divinum cultum directe ordinatum, non ad agendum peccatum, quamvis homo ex fomitis corruptione, ex occasione movetur ad vitium, audito legis præcepto, et justum, quoniam docet et imperat unicuique dare quod suum est, et injustitiam digne ulciscitur, et bonum, quia ad ultimum finem, qui optimus est, dirigit. Hinc ait Psalmista : Lex Domini immaculata, convertens animas, etc. Et Salomon : Mandatum lucerna est, et lex lux, et via vitæ increpatio disciplinæ.
paras.en: Further, the Apostle concludes from what has been said: [[7:12|Wherefore the law indeed|Itaque lex quidem]], the written law, [[7:12|is holy|sancta]], because it forbids vices and commands what is honourable. Hence, according to Isidore, law is a holy ordinance, commanding what is honourable. [[7:12|and the commandment|Et mandatum]] of the law is [[7:12|holy|sanctum]], that is, directly ordained to the worship of God, not to the doing of sin, although man, from the corruption of the tinder, is moved to vice by occasion when he hears the precept of the law; [[7:12|and just|et justum]], since it teaches and commands that each be given what is his, and duly punishes injustice; [[7:12|and good|et bonum]], because it directs to the last end, which is best. Hence the Psalmist says: [[Ps 18:8|The law of the Lord is unspotted, converting souls|Lex Domini immaculata, convertens animas]], etc. And Solomon: [[Prov 6:23|the commandment is a lamp, and the law a light, and reproofs of instruction are the way of life|Mandatum lucerna est, et lex lux, et via vitæ increpatio disciplinæ]].

paras.t: Ex his infert Apostolus quod sequi videtur, et tamen secundum veritatem non sequitur. Quod ergo bonum est, id est legis mandatum in se bonum consistens, mihi factum est mors, id est causa spiritualis necis? Dixit enim mandatum esse ad mortem, et per mandatum revixisse peccatum. Absit, id est, istud non sequitur. Quamvis enim per mandatum revixerit culpa, hoc tamen non per se, neque ex injustitia legis, sed malitia hominis, bono ex occasione abutentis. Ideo additur : Sed peccatum, id est concupiscentia vel fomes, ut appareat peccatum, id est, sciatur esse illicita ; vel, ut peccatum intus latens, foras erumpat ac pateat ; per bonum, id est per legem, non directe, sed ex occasione, operatum est mihi mortem, id est, ad mortale peccatum induxit me, privans me gratia Dei animam vivificante. Dato quippe mandato, magis inflammata est concupiscentia magisque provocata est contra hominem tentatoris invidia atque suggestio. Ut fiat supra modum consuetum, et ultra mensuram, peccans peccatum, id est concupiscentia nos peccare faciens, ita quod concupiscentia facit magis peccare sub lege quam ante, per mandatum, occasione, sicut expositum est. Vel sic : Ut fiat supra modum peccans peccatum per mandatum, id est, actuale peccatum ex fomite nascens, quo Deum offendimus, modum excedat per mandatum. Nam idem peccatum, lege accedente, gravius est quam ante; et quod ante erat tantummodo peccatum seu culpa, postmodum etiam prævaricatio est, id est divinæ legis transgressio. Propterea fit supra modum peccans peccatum, quia diversis de causis displicet Deo, et variis modis adversatur justitiæ.
paras.en: From this the Apostle draws a conclusion which seems to follow, and yet in truth does not follow. [[7:13|Was that then which is good|Quod ergo bonum est]], that is, the commandment of the law, which is good in itself, [[7:13|made death unto me|mihi factum est mors]], that is, the cause of spiritual death? For he said that the commandment was unto death, and that sin revived through the commandment. [[7:13|God forbid|Absit]], that is, that does not follow. For though guilt revived through the commandment, this was not of itself, nor from any injustice of the law, but from the malice of man, abusing what is good by occasion. So it is added: [[7:13|But sin|Sed peccatum]], that is, concupiscence or the tinder, [[7:13|that it may appear sin|ut appareat peccatum]], that is, that it may be known to be unlawful; or, that sin lying hidden within may break out and be plain; [[7:13|by that which is good|per bonum]], that is, by the law, not directly but by occasion, [[7:13|wrought death in me|operatum est mihi mortem]], that is, led me into mortal sin, depriving me of the grace of God which gives life to the soul. For once the commandment was given, concupiscence was more inflamed, and the envy and suggestion of the tempter more provoked against man. [[7:13|might become sinful above measure|Ut fiat supra modum]], above its usual measure and beyond bounds, [[7:13|that sin|peccans peccatum]] [*peccans peccatum*, literally "sinning sin": Denis takes it here as "sin that makes us sin"], that is, concupiscence which makes us sin, so that concupiscence makes us sin more under the law than before, [[7:13|by the commandment|per mandatum]], by occasion, as has been explained. Or thus: that sin, sinning by the commandment, may become above measure: that is, that actual sin, springing from the tinder, by which we offend God, may exceed measure by the commandment. For the same sin is graver once the law has come than before; and what before was only sin or guilt is afterwards also prevarication, that is, transgression of the divine law. So sin becomes sinful above measure, because it displeases God for various reasons and opposes justice in various ways.

paras.t: Deinde manifestat Apostolus legem esse spiritualem, id est carnales atque illicitas concupiscentias prohibentem. Scimus enim quia lex spiritualis est : quia et data est a Spiritu Sancto per spiritum angelicum, quatenus lege accepta, viveret homo secundum spiritum, non secundum carnem; ego autem carnalis sum, carnaliter vivens, passionum inclinationes sequendo. Loquitur autem Apostolus, sicut jam dictum est, in persona hominis generaliter. Nunc enim loquitur in persona ejus in quo invenitur peccans peccatum supra modum, hominis scilicet qui legem transgreditur. Quasi dicat : Quamvis ego carnalis sim, nihilo minus lex spiritualis est. Itaque, Carnalis sum, venundatus, id est damnationi seu dæmonis potestati ac juri, vel miseræ servituti, expositus atque obnoxius factus, sub peccato primi parentis, qui se ipsum et posteritatem suam vendidit hosti, faciendo quod ille proposuit. Vel potius, Sub peccato actuali et proprio, id est peccatorum meorum demerito : sicut per Isaiam Dominus profitetur. Ecce in iniquitatibus vestris venditi estis; et dictum est Achab : Venundatus es ut faceres malum coram Domino. Vendit namque se homo libero arbitrio, et recipit pro pretio vile bonum ab adversario suo.
paras.en: Next the Apostle shows that the law is spiritual, that is, that it forbids carnal and unlawful desires. [[7:14|For we know that the law is spiritual|Scimus enim quia lex spiritualis est]]: because it was given by the Holy Ghost through the ministry of angels[[Acts 7:53||]], so that, having received the law, man might live according to the spirit, not according to the flesh; [[7:14|But I am carnal|ego autem carnalis sum]], living carnally, following the inclinations of the passions. The Apostle speaks, as has been said already, in the person of man in general. For he now speaks in the person of one in whom sin is found sinning above measure, namely of a man who transgresses the law. As if he said: Though I am carnal, the law is none the less spiritual. So: I am carnal, [[7:14|sold|venundatus]], that is, exposed and made liable to damnation, or to the power and right of the devil, or to wretched slavery, [[7:14|under sin|sub peccato]] of our first parent, who sold himself and his posterity to the enemy by doing what he proposed. Or rather, under sin actual and one's own, that is, by the demerit of my own sins: as the Lord declares through Isaias: [[Is 50:1|behold you are sold for your iniquities|Ecce in iniquitatibus vestris venditi estis]]; and it was said to Achab: [[3 Kings 21:20|thou art sold, to do evil in the sight of the Lord|Venundatus es ut faceres malum coram Domino]] [the margin gives the chapter only, 3 Kings xxi]. For man sells himself by free will, and receives from his adversary a worthless good as the price.

paras.t: Quod enim operor in quantum carnalis, videlicet sensualitatem sequendo, non intelligo, id est, non vere considero, nec recte attendo. Nullus enim respiciens ad malum operatur, secundum Dionysium. Unde malum nec agitur, neque appetitur, nisi sub ratione boni. Propter quod Salomon ait : Omnis viri via recta sibi videtur. Vel, Non intelligo, id est, intus non lego tale malum tanquam rationi consonum. Non enim quod volo bonum, id est actum virtuosum, quem secundum rationis dictamen volo et approbo, hoc ago, quia carnalitati vitiisque succumbo; sed quod odi malum, id est peccatum quod secundum rationis censuram detestor, illud facio, passionibus cedens, et sensualitati consentiens. Si autem quod nolo secundum rationem, illud facio secundum sensualitatem : consentio legi, quoniam bona est, id est, legem approbo, quia quod illa prohibet, ratio mea malum esse cognoscit. Nunc autem, id est istis sic stantibus, jam non ego operor illud malum, in quantum homo seu rationalis creatura, cujus est vitia abhorrere, virtutes diligere, et deprecari ad optima, sed quod habitat in me peccatum, id est, fomes peccati, seu concupiscentia firmiter radicata in me, est causa mali, impellendo ad ipsum. Tanquam dicat : Non ut rationalis, sed ut brutalis seu bestiis similis, ago hoc malum, quod ratio reprobat.
paras.en: [[7:15|For that which I work|Quod enim operor]] in so far as I am carnal, namely by following sensuality, [[7:15|I understand not|non intelligo]], that is, I do not truly consider it, nor rightly attend to it. For no one acts looking to evil, according to Dionysius. Hence evil is neither done nor desired except under the aspect of good. For this reason Solomon says: [[Prov 21:2|Every way of a man seemeth right to himself|Omnis viri via recta sibi videtur]]. Or: I understand not, that is, I do not read inwardly [*intus lego*, Denis's play on *intelligo*] such evil as agreeing with reason. [[7:15|For I do not that good which I will|non enim quod volo bonum, hoc ago]], that is, the virtuous act which I will and approve according to the dictate of reason, because I give way to carnality and vices; [[7:15|but the evil which I hate|sed quod odi malum]], that is, the sin which I detest according to the judgment of reason, [[7:15|that I do|illud facio]], yielding to the passions and consenting to sensuality. [[7:16|If then I do that which I will not|Si autem quod nolo]] according to reason, I do according to sensuality: [[7:16|I consent to the law, that it is good|consentio legi, quoniam bona est]], that is, I approve the law, because what it forbids my reason knows to be evil. [[7:17|Now then|Nunc autem]], that is, things being so, [[7:17|it is no more I that do it|jam non ego operor illud]], the evil, in so far as I am a man or rational creature, whose part it is to abhor vices, love virtues and pray for what is best, [[7:17|but sin that dwelleth in me|sed quod habitat in me peccatum]], that is, the tinder of sin, or concupiscence firmly rooted in me, is the cause of the evil, driving me to it. As if he said: not as rational, but as brutish or like the beasts, I do this evil, which reason condemns.

paras.t: Ad horum intelligentiam pleniorem habendam, oportet advertere quod Apostolus assumit hoc loco personam duorum hominum, scilicet interioris, et exterioris; vel potius duplicis hominis, id est ejusdem secundum duplicem portionem ipsius. Est enim in homine duplex pars, videlicet intellectiva et sensitiva, seu ratio et sensualitas, quæ aliter appellantur spiritus et caro, homo interior atque exterior. Ratio autem competit homini secundum propriam hominis definitionem, sensualitas vero secundum id quod cum brutis communicat. Idcirco quod agit et vult secundum rationem, hoc dicitur proprie velle et agere. Hoc enim agit et vult secundum quod homo. Quod vero agit aut appetit secundum sensualitatem, seu partem sensitivam, sine rationis advertentia seu consensu, non dicitur proprie agere sive appetere, quia non agit, nec appetit illud in quantum homo, sed ut jumentis communicans. Sicque apparet quomodo homo dicitur agere quod tamen non agit, sicut jam dixit Apostolus : Quod nolo facio, et jam ego non operor illud. Denique non ita intelligendum est quod ait, Jam non ego operor illud, sed quod habitat in me peccatum, quasi homo nequaquam operetur illud, vel a vitio excusetur, sed quia non agit illud ut homo bene dispositus.
paras.en: For a fuller understanding of these things it must be noted that the Apostle here takes on the person of two men, namely the inner and the outer; or rather of a twofold man, that is, of the same man according to his twofold portion. For in man there is a twofold part, namely the intellective and the sensitive, or reason and sensuality, which are otherwise called spirit and flesh, the inner and the outer man. Reason belongs to man according to the proper definition of man, sensuality according to what he shares with the brutes. Therefore what he does and wills according to reason is properly said to be willed and done by him, for he does and wills it as a man. But what he does or desires according to sensuality, or the sensitive part, without the advertence or consent of reason, he is not properly said to do or desire, because he does not do or desire it as a man, but as one who shares with the beasts. And so it appears how a man is said to do what yet he does not do, as the Apostle has just said: [[7:16|I do that which I will not|Quod nolo facio]], and [[7:17|it is no more I that do it|jam ego non operor illud]]. Lastly, his words, [[7:17|it is no more I that do it: but sin that dwelleth in me|Jam non ego operor illud, sed quod habitat in me peccatum]], are not to be understood as if the man did not do it at all, or were excused from fault, but in that he does not do it as a well-ordered man.

paras.t: Scio enim, per experientiam reluctationis sensualitatis contra rationem, quia non habitat in me, hoc est in carne mea, videlicet in homine exteriori et parte sensitiva, bonum, id est virtus, seu habitus ad bonum inclinans, sed potius ad oppositum. Per hoc autem quod ait, Hoc est in carne mea, insinuat quod in parte intellectiva habitet bonum, puta synderesis, quæ remurmurat malo, et tendit in bonum. Ideo subdit : Nam velle adjacet mihi, id est, secundum hominem interiorem inclinor ad bona, et volo honesta ; perficere autem bonum, id est opere adimplere, non invenio in me, quoniam sine gratia illud non valeo, maxime propter rebellionem sensualitatis. Non enim quod volo bonum, hoc facio ; sed quod nolo malum, hoc ago. Si autem quod nolo, illud facio; jam non ego operor illud, sed quod habitat in me peccatum. Hæc jam præhabita atque exposita sunt.
paras.en: [[7:18|For I know|Scio enim]], by experience of the struggle of sensuality against reason, [[7:18|that there dwelleth not in me, that is to say, in my flesh|quia non habitat in me, hoc est in carne mea]], namely in the outer man and the sensitive part, [[7:18|that which is good|bonum]], that is, virtue, or a habit inclining to good, but rather to the opposite. By saying, [[7:18|that is to say, in my flesh|Hoc est in carne mea]], he hints that good dwells in the intellective part: synderesis, for instance [the natural habit of the first principles of moral action, the spark of conscience], which murmurs against evil and tends to good. So he adds: [[7:18|For to will is present with me|Nam velle adjacet mihi]], that is, according to the inner man I am inclined to good things and will what is honourable; [[7:18|but to accomplish that which is good|perficere autem bonum]], that is, to fulfil it in deed, [[7:18|I find not|non invenio]] in me, since without grace I cannot do it, chiefly because of the rebellion of sensuality. [[7:19|For the good which I will, I do not: but the evil which I will not, that I do.|Non enim quod volo bonum, hoc facio: sed quod nolo malum, hoc ago.]] [[7:20|Now if I do that which I will not, it is no more I that do it: but sin that dwelleth in me.|Si autem quod nolo, illud facio: jam non ego operor illud, sed quod habitat in me, peccatum.]] These things have been treated and explained already.

paras.t: Ex his infert Apostolus legem scriptam esse bonam, quoniam ratio naturalis ei consentit. Invenio igitur legem, volenti mihi facere bonum, id est, quum bona agere cupio, invenio legem, tam naturalem quam scriptam, consonam mihi bona volenti. Ex quo sequitur legem esse bonam. Quoniam mihi malum, id est pronitas ad peccandum, adjacet, id est, in promptu est. Pronior enim sum ad mala quam ad bona, propter corruptionem naturæ. Tanquam dicat : Ideo volo bonum, et erigo me contra me ipsum, quoniam cerno me ad mala proclivem, cui proclivitati cupio resistere. Condelector enim, id est, consentio, et delectabiliter afficior, legi Dei, volens quod præcipit, nolens quod prohibet, secundum interiorem hominem, id est secundum rationis judicium. Nam et lex naturalis legi divinæ concordat, præcipue quoad præcepta moralia. Lex quippe scripta, tam divina quam humana, est quædam determinatio, vel renovatio, seu explicatio legis naturalis, et comparatur ad eam sicut conclusio ad præmissas. Unde præcepta dicuntur esse de conclusionibus, non de primis principiis. Intentio autem præceptorum moralium est, hominem juste ordinare quantum ad Deum, et quantum ad proximum. Hæc vero præcepta determinantur dupliciter, scilicet, per præcepta cærimonialia, quæ assignant speciales modos colendi Deum, et per præcepta judicialia, quæ assignant aptum modum servandi justitiam inter homines. Hæc itaque duo genera præceptorum, non sunt de naturali dictamine rationis, sed ex institutione vim habent; nec sunt eadem ubique et semper, sed variantur apud diversos, secundum exigentiam personarum, locorum ac temporum.
paras.en: From this the Apostle concludes that the written law is good, since natural reason agrees with it. [[7:21|I find then a law, that when I have a will to do good|Invenio igitur legem, volenti mihi facere bonum]], that is, when I desire to do good things, I find a law, natural as well as written, in harmony with me as I will good things. From which it follows that the law is good. [[7:21|evil|Quoniam mihi malum]], that is, a proneness to sin, [[7:21|is present with me|adjacet]], that is, is at hand. For I am more prone to evil than to good, because of the corruption of nature. As if he said: I will good, and rise up against myself, because I see that I am inclined to evil, and I desire to resist that inclination. [[7:22|For I am delighted|Condelector enim]], that is, I consent and am affected with delight, [[7:22|with the law of God|legi Dei]], willing what it commands, not willing what it forbids, [[7:22|according to the inward man|secundum interiorem hominem]], that is, according to the judgment of reason. For the natural law too agrees with the divine law, chiefly as regards the moral precepts. For written law, divine as well as human, is a kind of determination, or renewal, or unfolding of the natural law, and is related to it as a conclusion to its premises. Hence precepts are said to be about conclusions, not about first principles. Now the intention of the moral precepts is to order man justly with regard to God and with regard to his neighbour. These precepts are determined in two ways: by the ceremonial precepts, which assign particular ways of worshipping God, and by the judicial precepts, which assign a fitting way of keeping justice among men. These two kinds of precepts, then, are not from the natural dictate of reason, but have their force from institution; nor are they the same everywhere and always, but vary among different peoples according to the needs of persons, places and times.

paras.t: Video autem aliam legem a lege Dei cui ratio condelectatur, in membris meis, id est in carne mea mortali, vitiata ac fragili, utpote fomitem peccati, qui primo respicit carnem et membrum generationis, et ex carnis contactu derivatur ad animam, quam cito corpori copulatur, repugnantem legi mentis meæ, id est legi naturali ac divinæ cordi meo inscriptæ, et captivantem me, id est, subjicientem per consuetudinem malam et consensum, in legem peccati quæ est in membris meis, id est sibi ipsi existenti in corporis membris, quæ universa in facta sunt promptitate ad malum. Captivat ergo lex membrorum hominem in sensualitate, quia pertrahit, et tenet in operibus ad quæ fomes inclinat. Lex autem dicitur a ligando, vel a legitima latione. Quoniam ergo fomes hominem in malo ligat, recte lex dicitur. Et etiam, quia legitime factum est ut caro repugnaret spiritui, quando spiritus inobediens exstitit Creatori. Homo enim in paradiso ante peccatum exsistens, sic conditus fuit ut quamdiu ipse per rationem esset subditus Deo, sensualitas subdita esset rationi, et caro spiritui : ita ut nec languor esset in anima, nec inordinata concupiscentia aut passio in sensualitate, stante subjectione rationis sub Deo. Et ut homo in tali conditione faciliter posset persistere, data et concreata erat ei originalis justitia, quæ erat rectitudo seu retinaculum quoddam habituale, tenens rationem sub Deo, sensualitatem sub ratione, et carnem sub anima. Unde ratione per inobedientiam a Deo aversa, mox orta est rebellio sensualitatis et carnis adversus spiritum. Et dispositio ad hanc rebellionem inclinans, vocatur fomes peccati, lexque membrorum.
paras.en: [[7:23|But I see another law|Video autem aliam legem]], other than the law of God in which reason delights, [[7:23|in my members|in membris meis]], that is, in my mortal flesh, corrupted and frail: namely the tinder of sin, which first concerns the flesh and the member of generation, and from contact with the flesh passes to the soul as soon as it is joined to the body; [[7:23|fighting against the law of my mind|repugnantem legi mentis meæ]], that is, against the natural and divine law written in my heart; [[7:23|and captivating me|et captivantem me]], that is, subjecting me through evil habit and consent, [[7:23|in the law of sin that is in my members|in legem peccati quæ est in membris meis]], that is, to itself, as it exists in the members of the body, all of which are infected with a readiness for evil. So the law of the members takes man captive in his sensuality, because it drags him to, and holds him in, the works to which the tinder inclines. Now law is named from binding, or from lawful enactment [*lex*, "law", from *ligare*, "to bind", or from *legitima latio*]. Since, then, the tinder binds man in evil, it is rightly called a law. And also because it came about lawfully [that is, justly] that the flesh should fight against the spirit, when the spirit became disobedient to the Creator. For man, existing in paradise before sin, was so made that as long as he himself was subject to God through reason, sensuality was subject to reason and the flesh to the spirit: so that there was neither weakness in the soul nor disordered desire or passion in sensuality, while reason remained subject to God. And so that man might easily persist in such a condition, original justice had been given him and created together with him: a rectitude, or a kind of habitual restraint, holding reason under God, sensuality under reason, and the flesh under the soul. Hence, when reason turned away from God by disobedience, there at once arose the rebellion of sensuality and of the flesh against the spirit. And the disposition inclining to this rebellion is called the tinder of sin, and the law of the members.

paras.t: Præterea ex consideratione tantæ miseriæ cui subjectus est homo, exclamat Apostolus : Infelix ego homo, privatus felicitate originalis justitiæ, multisque corruptionibus et vitiis plenus! quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus, id est, de corpore isto mortali, quod obligat ad mortem naturæ, inclinat ad mortem culpæ, exponitque periculis mortis æternæ, quatenus anima mea hac vitæ subtracta, ad patriam redeat, et Deo libere perfruatur, secureque vivat? Et respondet : Gratia Dei Trinitatis per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum, per quem gratia Dei nobis infunditur ac præstatur. Hanc ergo liberationem desiderabilem animæ a corpore facit Deus effective, gratia Dei formaliter, Christus homo meritorie.
paras.en: Further, considering the great misery to which man is subject, the Apostle cries out: [[7:24|Unhappy man that I am|Infelix ego homo]], deprived of the happiness of original justice, and full of many corruptions and vices! [[7:24|who shall deliver me from the body of this death|quis me liberabit de corpore mortis hujus]], that is, from this mortal body, which binds me to the death of nature, inclines me to the death of guilt, and exposes me to the dangers of eternal death: so that my soul, withdrawn from this life, may return to the fatherland, enjoy God freely, and live secure? And he answers: [[7:25|The grace of God|Gratia Dei]], the Trinity, [[7:25|by Jesus Christ our Lord|per Jesum Christum Dominum nostrum]], through whom the grace of God is poured into us and bestowed on us. This longed-for deliverance of the soul from the body, then, God works as its efficient cause, the grace of God as its formal cause, and Christ as man as its meritorious cause.

paras.t: Sed quum alibi dicat Apostolus, Nolumus exspoliari, sed supervestiri ; et, Nemo carnem suam unquam odio habuit : quomodo nunc cupit liberari a corpore? Et respondendum, quod liberatio ista intelligi potest dupliciter : Primo, per separationem animæ a corpore. Sicque Apostolus et alii Sancti optaverunt a corpore liberari, per mortem temporalem, desiderio Christi ac patriæ, sicut alio loco habetur : Cupio dissolvi, et esse cum Christo. Pro hac quoque liberatione oravit Psalmista : Educ, inquiens, de custodia animam meam ad confitendum nomini tuo ; et iterum, Heu mihi ! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est; et, Quando veniam, et apparebo ante conspectum Dei? Secundo, intelligi potest per separationem corporis a mortalitate, ceterisque afflictionibus, et miseriis, et peccatis. Sic autem optant electi liberari a corpore mortis in die judicii, scilicet, ut resurgant in corpore glorificato, non passibili et misero. Tunc enim liberabuntur corpora Sanctorum ab omnibus malis prædictis. Unde Apostolus non ait simpliciter, De corpore, sed, De corpore mortis. Et ita nolumus finaliter exspoliari, sed ad tempus, quatenus in resurrectione futura supervestiamur impassibili corpore, quod erit ornamentum, non onus.
paras.en: But since elsewhere the Apostle says, [[2 Cor 5:4|we would not be unclothed, but clothed upon|Nolumus exspoliari, sed supervestiri]]; and, [[Eph 5:29|no man ever hated his own flesh|Nemo carnem suam unquam odio habuit]]: how does he now desire to be delivered from the body? The answer is that this deliverance can be understood in two ways. First, by the separation of the soul from the body. In this way the Apostle and other Saints longed to be delivered from the body by temporal death, out of desire for Christ and the fatherland, as is said in another place: I desire [[Phil 1:23|to be dissolved and to be with Christ|dissolvi, et esse cum Christo]]. For this deliverance too the Psalmist prayed, saying: [[Ps 141:8|Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name|Educ, inquiens, de custodia animam meam ad confitendum nomini tuo]]; and again, [[Ps 119:5|Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged|Heu mihi ! quia incolatus meus prolongatus est]]; and, [[Ps 41:3|when shall I come and appear before the face of God|Quando veniam, et apparebo ante conspectum Dei]]? Secondly, it can be understood of the separation of the body from mortality and the other afflictions and miseries and sins. In this way the elect long to be delivered from the body of death on the day of judgment: namely, to rise in a glorified body, not one subject to suffering and misery. For then the bodies of the Saints will be delivered from all the evils just named. Hence the Apostle does not say simply, from the body, but [[7:24|from the body of this death|de corpore mortis]]. And so we would not be unclothed for good, but for a time, so that in the resurrection to come we may be clothed upon with an impassible body, which will be an ornament, not a burden.

paras.t: Ex dictis concludit Apostolus : Igitur ego ipse mente, id est secundum rationem, servio legi Dei ; carnem autem, id est secundum carnis et fomitis inclinationem, servio legi peccati, quæ est in membris. Si in sui ipsius persona hoc dicit Apostolus, referendum est ad peccata venialia ac minutissima, quibus forte interdum non caruit, vel ad statum quem habebat sub lege Mosaica. Servire autem legi peccati, est inclinationibus fomitis consentire.
paras.en: From what has been said the Apostle concludes: [[7:25|Therefore, I myself, with the mind|Igitur ego ipse mente]], that is, according to reason, [[7:25|serve the law of God|servio legi Dei]]; [[7:25|but with the flesh|carnem autem]], that is, according to the inclination of the flesh and the tinder, I serve [[7:25|the law of sin|legi peccati]], which is in the members. If the Apostle says this in his own person, it is to be referred to venial and very small sins, from which perhaps he was not always free, or to the state he was in under the Mosaic law. Now to serve the law of sin is to consent to the inclinations of the tinder.

8.title: EXPLANATIO CAPITULI OCTAVI : NIHIL ERGO NUNC DAMNATIONIS EST, ETC.
8.title_en: Explanation of the eighth chapter: There is now therefore no condemnation, etc.

paras.t: DECLARATA in præcedenti capitulo cessatione legis Mosaicæ, jam docet Christo et evangelicæ legi jugiter inhærendum, et ait : Nihil ergo nunc, scilicet tempore gratiæ, damnationis, id est obligationis ad pœnam gehennæ, est his qui sunt in Christo Jesu per fidem et caritatem : quibus ipse loquitur, Manete in me, et ego in vobis ; qui non secundum carnem ambulant, id est, carnis desideriis non acquiescunt, neque carnaliter vivunt, sed carnem cum vitiis et concupiscentiis crucifigunt. In fonte namque Baptismatis dimissa sunt eis peccata universa. Si autem postea non peccaverunt, manendo in Christo proferunt fructum multum, et ita non tantum pro vitiis satisfaciunt, sed insuper gloriam ampliorem merentur. Lex enim spiritus vitæ, id est lex evangelica : quæ nominatur lex spiritus, quia a Spiritu Sancto est data, Christianorumque cordibus ab ipso impressa; dicitur quoque lex vitæ, quoniam mentem vivificat, per gratiam quam sacramenta novæ legis distribuunt; in Christo Jesu, id est per Christum, liberavit me a lege peccati et mortis, id est a consensu, consuetudine, et actu culpæ ac pœnæ pro culpa infligendæ. Potest quoque per legem peccati, lex scripta intelligi, eo quod ex occasione auxerit culpam ac pœnam, quemadmodum in superioribus ubertim expositum est.
paras.en: Having in the preceding chapter set forth the ceasing of the Mosaic law, he now teaches that we must cleave constantly to Christ and to the law of the Gospel, and says: [[8:1|There is now therefore|Nihil ergo nunc]], that is, in the time of grace, [[8:1|no condemnation|damnationis]], that is, no liability to the punishment of hell, [[8:1|to them that are in Christ Jesus|est his qui sunt in Christo Jesu]] by faith and charity: to whom He Himself says, [[John 15:4|Abide in me: and I in you|Manete in me, et ego in vobis]]; [[8:1|who walk not according to the flesh|qui non secundum carnem ambulant]], that is, who do not yield to the desires of the flesh nor live carnally, but crucify the flesh with its vices and concupiscences[[Gal 5:24||]]. For in the font of Baptism all their sins were forgiven them. And if afterwards they have not sinned, by abiding in Christ they bring forth much fruit[[John 15:5||]], and so not only make satisfaction for their faults, but moreover merit greater glory. [[8:2|For the law of the spirit of life|Lex enim spiritus vitæ]], that is, the law of the Gospel: which is called the law of the spirit because it was given by the Holy Ghost and imprinted by Him on the hearts of Christians; and it is called the law of life because it quickens the mind through the grace which the sacraments of the new law dispense; [[8:2|in Christ Jesus|in Christo Jesu]], that is, through Christ, [[8:2|hath delivered me from the law of sin and of death|liberavit me a lege peccati et mortis]], that is, from the consent, the habit and the act of guilt, and from the punishment to be inflicted for guilt. By the law of sin may also be understood the written law, in that it occasionally increased guilt and punishment, as was set forth at length above[[Rom 7:8||]].

paras.t: Proinde declarat Apostolus, quomodo lex Christi, quæ est lex spiritus vitæ, liberet a lege peccati et mortis. Nam quod impossibile erat legi scriptæ et sacramentis ipsius, non continentibus nec conferentibus gratiam, in quo infirmabatur, id est, in qua impossibilitate atque inefficacia, infirma et ad salvandum impotens erat lex ipsa, per carnem, id est per observantias et justificationes carnales, quæ non purificant animam. Sacramenta enim legalia corporaliter tantum mundabant, quasdam inhabilitates seu irregularitates ab exteriori inductas, et ab ingressu templi atque similibus impedientes, tollendo. Vel, Per carnem, id est per fomitem carnis, quem lex occasionaliter incitavit, non directe diminuit. Deus Pater Filium suum mittens in mundum per incarnationis mysterium, non per localem descensum, in similitudinem carnis peccati, id est in corpore mortali atque passibili : quod licet fuerit veraciter veraque caro, non tamen veraciter erat caro peccati, sed similitudinarie. Per pœnas enim quas pertulit, similis erat carni peccatrici. Venit itaque Christus in veritate carnis, non autem in veritate carnis peccati, sed in similitudine ejus.
paras.en: Next the Apostle shows how the law of Christ, which is the law of the spirit of life, delivers from the law of sin and of death. [[8:3|For what the law could not do|Nam quod impossibile erat legi]], the written law and its sacraments, which neither contained nor conferred grace, [[8:3|in that it was weak|in quo infirmabatur]], that is, in which impossibility and inefficacy the law itself was weak and powerless to save, [[8:3|through the flesh|per carnem]], that is, through carnal observances and justifications, which do not purify the soul. For the legal sacraments cleansed only bodily, by removing certain disabilities or irregularities contracted from without, which barred from entering the temple and the like. Or, through the flesh, that is, through the fomes of the flesh [the inclination to sin left in fallen nature], which the law occasionally stirred up and did not directly lessen. [[8:3|God, sending his own Son|Deus Pater Filium suum mittens]] (God the Father) into the world through the mystery of the Incarnation, not by a descent in place, [[8:3|in the likeness of sinful flesh|in similitudinem carnis peccati]], that is, in a mortal and passible body: which, though it was truly and really flesh, was not truly flesh of sin, but only by likeness. For through the penalties which He bore He was like to sinful flesh. Christ therefore came in the reality of flesh, but not in the reality of sinful flesh, only in its likeness.

paras.t: Et de peccato damnavit peccatum : id est, Pater mittens sic Filium, damnavit, id est, delevit, destruxit, dimisit peccatum, tam originale quam actuale, de peccato, id est per peccatum factum in carne Christi, non a Christo, sed a diabolo ejusque ministris qui Christum occiderunt. Per hoc enim quod Christus injuste occisus est, suggerente diabolo, amisit diabolus jus quod habebat in nobis, et ita mors Christo inique illata, omne peccatum delevit. Vel : Damnavit peccatum actuale, nascens de peccato, id est fomite peccati ; vel, Peccatum de peccato, id est fomitem peccati, procedentem de peccato originali Adæ. Vel sic, et melius, secundum Ambrosium : De peccato, id est de se ipso, prout factus est hostia pro peccato nostro, damnavit, id est delevit, peccatum mundi quodcumque, in carne, id est in corporis sui passione. Ipse enim portavit peccata nostra in corpore suo super lignum. Juxta hunc sensum sacrificia legis pro peccatis oblata, dicebantur peccata, secundum quod de sacerdotibus veteris Testamenti Dominus ait per Osee : Peccata populi mei comedent. Sic quoque aquam cum periculo vitæ allatam David, sanguinem appellavit, dicens : Absit a me, ut sanguinem virorum istorum bibam.
paras.en: [[8:3|and of sin, hath condemned sin|et de peccato, damnavit peccatum]]: that is, the Father, sending the Son thus, condemned, that is, blotted out, destroyed, remitted sin, original as well as actual, of sin, that is, by the sin committed [[8:3|in the flesh|in carne]] of Christ, not by Christ, but by the devil and his ministers who slew Christ. For because Christ was unjustly slain at the devil's prompting, the devil lost the right he had over us, and so the death wickedly inflicted on Christ blotted out all sin. Or: He condemned actual sin, springing of sin, that is, of the fomes of sin; or, sin of sin, that is, the fomes of sin proceeding from the original sin of Adam. Or thus, and better, according to Ambrose: Of sin, that is, of Himself, inasmuch as He was made a victim for our sin, He condemned, that is, blotted out, every sin of the world, in the flesh, that is, in the passion of His body. For [[1 Pet 2:24|Who his own self bore our sins in his body upon the tree|Ipse … portavit … super lignum]]. In this sense the sacrifices of the law offered for sins were called sins, as the Lord says through Osee of the priests of the Old Testament: [[Osee 4:8|They shall eat the sins of my people|Peccata populi mei comedent]] [Denis's word order differs slightly from the Vulgate]. So too David called the water brought at peril of life blood, saying: [[1 Par 11:19|God forbid that I should do this in the sight of my God, and should drink the blood of these men|Absit a me, ut sanguinem virorum istorum bibam]].

paras.t: Hæc itaque fecit Deus, ut justificatio legis, id est in lege promissa, non autem per legem exhibita : lex enim gratiam justificantem spopondit, non contulit: impleretur in nobis, qui in Baptismo aliisque sacramentis gratiam justificantem in lege præfiguratam ac prænuntiatam recipimus, qui non secundum carnem ambulamus, sed secundum spiritum, id est, non carnaliter, sed spiritualiter in hujus vitæ exsilio conversamur, tendentes ac properantes ad patriam per opera virtuosa. De hac legis promissione aiebat Apostolus loquens de Judæis : Et nos vobis annuntiamus eam quæ ad patres nostros facta est repromissio, quoniam hanc Deus implevit filiis nostris. Hinc etiam Petrus in sua Canonica : De qua salute exquisierunt atque scrutati sunt Prophetæ, qui de futura in vobis gratia prophetaverunt : quibus revelatum est quia non sibi ipsis, vobis autem ministraverunt ea quæ nunc nuntiata sunt vobis.
paras.en: These things, then, God did [[8:4|That the justification of the law|ut justificatio legis]], that is, promised in the law, but not bestowed through the law (for the law promised justifying grace but did not confer it), [[8:4|might be fulfilled in us|impleretur in nobis]], who in Baptism and the other sacraments receive the justifying grace prefigured and foretold in the law, [[8:4|who walk not according to the flesh, but according to the spirit|qui non secundum carnem ambulamus, sed secundum spiritum]], that is, who live in the exile of this life not carnally but spiritually, tending and hastening to the fatherland by virtuous works. Of this promise of the law the Apostle said, speaking of the Jews: [[Acts 13:32|And we declare unto you that the promise which was made|Et nos vobis annuntiamus eam quæ ad patres nostros facta est]], [[Acts 13:33|This same God hath fulfilled to our children|quoniam hanc Deus implevit filiis nostris]]. Hence also Peter in his Canonical Epistle: [[1 Pet 1:10|Of which salvation the prophets have inquired and diligently searched, who prophesied of the grace to come in you|De qua salute exquisierunt atque scrutati sunt Prophetæ, qui de futura in vobis]] [[1 Pet 1:12|To whom it was revealed that, not to themselves but to you, they ministered those things which are now declared to you|quibus revelatum est quia non sibi ipsis, vobis autem ministraverunt ea quæ nunc nuntiata sunt vobis]].

paras.t: Pro intellectu loci hujus intricati atque difficilis advertendum, quod nemo unquam salvatus est nisi per fidem et gratiam Christi. Ipse enim est caput omnium electorum ; membra autem necesse est capiti counire, ut vitam participent. Propter quod Petrus disserebat : Nec enim aliud nomen sub cœlo datum est hominibus, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri. Passio namque Christi hoc fecit futura, quod facit impleta.
paras.en: For the understanding of this intricate and difficult passage, note that no one was ever saved except through faith in Christ and His grace. For He is the head of all the elect[[Eph 1:22||]]; and the members must be united to the head in order to share its life. Wherefore Peter declared: [[Acts 4:12|For there is no other name under heaven given to men, whereby we must be saved|Nec enim aliud nomen sub cœlo datum est hominibus, in quo oporteat nos salvos fieri]]. For the passion of Christ, while yet to come, did the same as it does now accomplished.

paras.t: Porro, hæc salus aliter applicatur hominibus post Christi passionem, et aliter ante. Tunc enim applicabatur per fidem formatam, nunc vero applicatur etiam per sacramenta gratiæ contentiva, effectiva et causativa. Potest autem aliquid movere vel agere, antequam sit in effectu, videlicet secundum quod est in apprehensione animæ, et dispositione causæ efficientis, quemadmodum finis movet agentem. Ad hoc autem quod aliquid agat et moveat in genere causæ efficientis, oportet ut sit, et effectum præcedat, eo quod causa effectiva non sit suo effectu posterior. Sacramenta ergo veteris legis et fides Christi venturi, habere non poterant quemlibet effectum dominicæ passionis, quem nunc habent sacramenta ac fides evangelicæ legis, quæ operantur virtute passionis dominicæ jam impletæ. Et ideo gratiam operantur, et a reatu originalis peccati absolvunt : quorum nullum sacramenta legis facere poterant. Unde omnes patres pro tunc descenderunt in limbum inferni. Nam licet per fidem et gratiam Dei, virtute passionis Christi et merito ejus futuro, absolverentur a pœna et culpa actualium peccatorum, non tamen a reatu originalis peccati.
paras.en: Now this salvation is applied to men in one way after Christ's passion and in another before it. Then it was applied through formed faith [that is, faith informed by charity]; now it is applied also through sacraments which contain, effect and cause grace. A thing can move or act before it exists in fact, namely inasmuch as it is in the apprehension of the mind and in the intention of the efficient cause, as the end moves the agent. But for a thing to act and move in the order of efficient cause, it must exist and precede the effect, since an efficient cause is not later than its effect. The sacraments of the old law, therefore, and faith in Christ to come, could not have every effect of the Lord's passion which the sacraments and faith of the Gospel law now have, which work by the power of the Lord's passion already accomplished. And so these work grace and absolve from the guilt of original sin, neither of which the sacraments of the law could do. Hence all the fathers of that time went down into the limbo of hell. For although through faith and the grace of God, by the power of Christ's passion and His merit yet to come, they were absolved from the punishment and guilt of actual sins, they were not absolved from the guilt of original sin.

paras.t: Ex quo innotescit, quod passio Christi fortius agit impleta, quam egit implenda. Quemadmodum enim sacramenta novæ legis, sunt causæ instrumentales nostræ salutis et gratiæ, quoniam agunt virtute et merito passionis dominicæ, suntque vasa medicinalia spiritualium unguentorum contentiva, animarum languores curantia ; sic humanitas seu passio Christi, est causa instrumentalis, effectiva et meritoria nostræ salutis et gratiæ. Utrumque vero est instrumentum divinitatis Christi. Divinitas namque est causa efficiens principalis, quæ agit per humanitatem assumptam sicut per instrumentum conjunctum, per sacramenta vero, sicut per instrumenta separata : quemadmodum medicus est causa sanitatis efficiens principalis, manus autem est sicut causa instrumentalis conjuncta, ignis vero quo medicina paratur, est causa instrumentalis separata. Causa autem instrumentalis quum est in effectu, vel quum causa ejus principalis jam est, fortius operatur quam ante. Hinc ergo ait Apostolus, quod Deus misit Filium suum, de peccato damnans peccatum, ut justificatio legis impleretur in nobis : quod impossibile erat legi, justificare non valenti, in quo lex infirmabatur, seu debilis erat. Et hoc modo construenda est littera.
paras.en: From this it appears that the passion of Christ acts more powerfully now accomplished than it acted when yet to be accomplished. For as the sacraments of the new law are instrumental causes of our salvation and grace, since they act by the power and merit of the Lord's passion, and are medicinal vessels containing spiritual ointments that heal the sicknesses of souls; so the humanity or passion of Christ is the instrumental, effective and meritorious cause of our salvation and grace. Both are instruments of the Godhead of Christ. For the Godhead is the principal efficient cause, acting through the assumed humanity as through a conjoined instrument, and through the sacraments as through separate instruments: as the physician is the principal efficient cause of health, the hand as a conjoined instrumental cause, and the fire with which the medicine is prepared a separate instrumental cause. And an instrumental cause, when it exists in fact, or when its principal cause already exists, works more powerfully than before. Hence the Apostle says that God sent His Son, condemning sin of sin, that the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us: which was impossible to the law, which could not justify, in which the law was weak or feeble. And in this way the text is to be construed.

paras.t: Quod autem justificatio legis non nisi in spiritualibus impleatur hominibus, liquet. Qui enim secundum carnem sunt, id est, qui carnaliter vivunt : qui utique attendunt se ipsos secundum esse suum carnale ac sensitivum, non secundum esse spirituale ac intellectivum ; quæ carnis sunt, sapiunt, id est, carnalia gustant, sensibilia ac temporalia cum sensualitatis sapore attendunt. Qui vero secundum spiritum, id est spiritualiter conversantes, et esse suum supremum, in quo Trinitatis imago relucet, pensantes, quæ sunt spiritus sentiunt, id est, spiritualia atque divina saporose intelligunt, delectabiliter pensant, sollicite implent, in talibus jugiter occupantur.
paras.en: That the justification of the law is fulfilled only in spiritual men is plain. [[8:5|For they that are according to the flesh|Qui enim secundum carnem sunt]], that is, who live carnally, who regard themselves according to their carnal and sensitive being, not according to their spiritual and intellectual being, [[8:5|mind the things that are of the flesh|quæ carnis sunt, sapiunt]], that is, relish carnal things, attend to sensible and temporal things with the savour of sensuality [the Latin *sapiunt*, “mind”, is akin to *sapor*, taste]. [[8:5|but they that are according to the spirit|Qui vero secundum spiritum]], that is, those who live spiritually and ponder their highest being, in which the image of the Trinity shines, [[8:5|mind the things that are of the spirit|quæ sunt spiritus, sentiunt]], that is, understand spiritual and divine things with relish, ponder them with delight, carry them out with care, and are constantly occupied in them.

paras.t: Nam prudentia carnis, id est carnalis ac sæcularis prudentia, mors est, id est mortale peccatum, inferens mortem culpæ in via, mortemque pœnæ in gehenna. Dicitur autem prudentia carnis hoc loco, per quam homo sibi in bonis carnalibus ac mundanis finem constituit, et ad talis finis adeptionem opera sua caute disponit. Hæc prudentia, non est vera prudentia, sed appellatur prudentia, propter apparentem similitudinem quam habet cum vera prudentia. Unde ait Salvator : Filii hujus sæculi prudentiores filiis lucis in generatione sua sunt ; et Jacobus, Non est ista sapientia (id est prudentia) a Deo, sed terrena, animalis et diabolica. Prudentia autem spiritus, id est vera ac spiritualis prudentia, quæ opera hominis convenienter disponit in ordine ad ultimum finem, est vita et pax, id est causa vitæ et pacis, in præsenti inchoative, in futuro perfecte. Nunc enim efficit in nobis vitam pacemque gratiæ, in patria vero meretur, vel potius adipiscitur, pacem et vitam gloriæ. Non distinguit Apostolus jam inter prudentiam et sapientiam. Proprie enim ad sapientiam spectat spiritualia sapere. De hac ergo spirituali prudentia, intelligendum est illud Jacobi : Quæ desursum est sapientia, primum quidem pudica est, deinde pacifica, modesta, suasibilis, bonis consentiens. Sciendum quoque quod pax directe ac proprie, est caritatis effectus, juxta illud in Psalmo : Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam. Est etiam pax effectus justitiæ, tanquam removentis impedimenta pacis. Propter quod per Isaiam dicitur : Erit opus justitiæ pax. Nunc vero dicitur pax esse effectus prudentiæ, tanquam dirigentis affectus nostros in viam pacis.
paras.en: [[8:6|For the wisdom of the flesh|Nam prudentia carnis]] [the Latin has *prudentia*, prudence], that is, carnal and worldly prudence, [[8:6|is death|mors est]], that is, mortal sin, bringing the death of guilt on the way and the death of punishment in hell. Here prudence of the flesh means that by which a man sets his end in carnal and worldly goods and cunningly orders his works to the attaining of such an end. This is not true prudence, but is called prudence because of its apparent likeness to true prudence. Hence the Saviour says: [[Luke 16:8|the children of this world are wiser in their generation than the children of light|Filii hujus sæculi prudentiores filiis lucis in generatione sua sunt]]; and James: [[Jas 3:15|For this is not wisdom|Non est ista sapientia]] (that is, prudence) [[Jas 3:15|descending from above: but earthly, sensual, devilish|a Deo, sed terrena, animalis et diabolica]]. [[8:6|but the wisdom of the spirit|Prudentia autem spiritus]], that is, true and spiritual prudence, which fitly orders a man's works to the last end, is [[8:6|life and peace|vita et pax]], that is, the cause of life and peace, begun in the present, perfect in the future. For now it works in us the life and peace of grace, and in the fatherland it merits, or rather attains, the peace and life of glory. The Apostle here does not distinguish between prudence and wisdom, though properly it belongs to wisdom to savour spiritual things. Of this spiritual prudence, then, is to be understood that saying of James: [[Jas 3:17|But the wisdom that is from above, first indeed is chaste, then peaceable, modest, easy to be persuaded, consenting to the good|Quæ desursum est sapientia, primum quidem pudica est, deinde pacifica, modesta, suasibilis, bonis consentiens]]. Know too that peace is directly and properly the effect of charity, according to the Psalm: [[Ps 118:165|Much peace have they that love thy law|Pax multa diligentibus legem tuam]]. Peace is also the effect of justice, as removing the hindrances of peace; wherefore it is said through Isaias: [[Is 32:17|And the work of justice shall be peace|Erit opus justitiæ pax]]. Here peace is said to be the effect of prudence, as directing our affections into the way of peace.

paras.t: Quoniam sapientia carnis inimica est Deo, id est divinæ voluntati atque sapientiæ veræ contraria. Ecce nunc loco prudentiæ ponit sapientiam : ex quo certum est, quod inter sapientiam et prudentiam non distinguit. Legi enim Dei non est subjecta sapientia ista carnalis, mundana ac vana, quia nec credit nec agit quæ lex divina tradit esse credenda sive agenda. Propter quod ait Salvator : Confiteor tibi, Pater, quia abscondisti hæc a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis ; et Jeremias, Sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nescierunt. Nec enim potest divinæ legi esse subjecta sapientia ista. Unum namque oppositorum non subjicitur alteri, sed repugnat. Lex autem divina docet ultimum finem esse constituendum in Deo, hæc vero in bonis carnalibus. Qui autem in carne sunt, id est, carnaliter vivunt, atque in sensibilibus bonis finaliter sistunt, Deo placere non possunt, in quantum hujusmodi. Possunt tamen converti, et Deo reconciliari. Huic dicto consonat illud Salvatoris : Nemo potest duobus dominis servire.
paras.en: [[8:7|Because the wisdom of the flesh is an enemy to God|Quoniam sapientia carnis inimica est Deo]], that is, contrary to the divine will and to true wisdom. See, he now puts wisdom in place of prudence; whence it is certain that he does not distinguish between them. [[8:7|For it is not subject to the law of God|Legi enim Dei non est subjecta]], this carnal, worldly and vain wisdom, because it neither believes nor does what the divine law teaches must be believed or done. Wherefore the Saviour says: [[Luke 10:21|I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because thou hast hidden these things from the wise and prudent and hast revealed them to little ones|Confiteor tibi, Pater, quia abscondisti hæc a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis]]; and Jeremias: [[Jer 4:22|they are wise to do evil, but to do good|Sapientes sunt ut faciant mala, bene autem facere nescierunt]]. [[8:7|neither can it be|Nec enim potest]] subject to the divine law, this wisdom. For one of two opposites is not subject to the other but resists it. The divine law teaches that the last end is to be placed in God, this wisdom places it in carnal goods. [[8:8|And they who are in the flesh|Qui autem in carne sunt]], that is, who live carnally and rest finally in sensible goods, [[8:8|cannot please God|Deo placere non possunt]], insofar as they are such. Yet they can be converted and reconciled to God. With this saying agrees that of the Saviour: [[Matt 6:24|No man can serve two masters|Nemo potest duobus dominis servire]].

paras.t: Vos autem, o veraciter Christifideles, in carne non estis, id est, in rebus ac vitiis carnis non detinemini, sed spiritualia atque divina exquiritis, conversationem habentes in cœlis, sed in spiritu, id est, in Spiritu Sancto estis, per caritatem et gratiam, et propter spiritualem regenerationem, qua estis ex aqua et Spiritu Sancto renati. Vel, Estis in spiritu vestro, id est secundum rationis judicium vivitis : juxta quod scriptum est, Redite, prævaricatores, ad cor. Si tamen Spiritus Dei, id est Spiritus Sanctus, habitat, id est manet, in vobis per gratiam gratum facientem : quemadmodum loquitur Christus, Ego rogabo Patrem, et alium Paracletum dabit vobis, ut maneat vobiscum in æternum. Rursusque ait : Spiritus Sanctus apud vos manebit, et in vobis erit. Si quis autem Spiritum Christi non habet, id est, cujus anima non habitatur a Spiritu Sancto : qui est Spiritus Christi, quia ab ipso procedit, ab eoque datur ac mittitur, sicut ipse protestatur. Quum venerit Paracletus, quem ego mittam vobis a Patre : et iterum, Ille de meo accipiet. Et ad hoc designandum, insufflavit in discipulos suos, et dixit : Accipite Spiritum Sanctum. Quis autem habet Spiritum Sanctum, nisi quietus et humilis, simplex et justus? Scriptum est enim : Super quem requiescet Spiritus meus, nisi super quietum et humilem? Et iterum : Spiritus Sanctus disciplinæ effugiet fictum, et auferet se a cogitationibus quæ sunt sine intellectu. Hic non est ejus, id est, ad membra Christi non pertinet, secundum præsentem justitiam et merito, quamvis interdum pertineat secundum prædestinationem æternam ac numero, sicut et Paulus quum Stephanum lapidavit.
