paras.t: Unde de diversitate donorum singulis concessorum, subjungitur : Habentes autem donationes, id est, sic singuli sumus membra alterius, sed habemus donationes secundum gratiam quæ data est nobis, differentes, id est dona distincta secundum gratiam majorem vel minorem nobis impensam. Unusquisque enim suum donum habet a Deo, alius quidem sic, alius vero sic, secundum quod misericordia et gratia Dei major est in uno quam in alio. Cetera quippe dona supernaturalia sive gratuita, mensuram gratiæ habitualis et primæ aliquo modo sequuntur. Deinde explicat dona ista diversis diversimode distributa. Sive prophetiam, id est revelationem secretorum, maxime futurorum, humanam rationem transcendentium, sumus habentes : et hoc, secundum rationem, id est secundum finem et exigentiam, fidei catholicæ. Prophetia namque ordinatur ad fidei roborationem, et proprie respicit ea quæ pertinent ad salutem, quæ est finis quem fides docet atque proponit. Ideo secundum fidei rationem prophetia confertur divinitus, et sic habetur a nobis.
paras.en: So, on the diversity of the gifts granted to each, it is added: [[12:6|And having different gifts|Habentes autem donationes secundum gratiam, quæ data est nobis, differentes]], that is, each of us is thus a member of the other, but we have gifts [[12:6|according to the grace that is given us|secundum gratiam quæ data est nobis]], different, that is, distinct gifts according to the greater or lesser grace bestowed on us. For [[1 Cor 7:7|every one hath his proper gift from God: one after this manner, and another after that|Unusquisque enim suum donum habet a Deo, alius quidem sic, alius vero sic]], according as the mercy and grace of God is greater in one than in another. For the other supernatural or gratuitous gifts follow in some way the measure of habitual and first grace. Then he sets out these gifts, distributed in different ways to different people. [[12:6|either prophecy|Sive prophetiam]], that is, the revelation of secrets, above all of things to come, that surpass human reason, if we have it: and this [[12:6|to be used according to the rule of faith|secundum rationem fidei]], that is, according to the end and the needs of the Catholic faith. For prophecy is ordained to strengthening the faith, and properly concerns what pertains to salvation, which is the end that faith teaches and sets before us. So prophecy is conferred by God, and is had by us, according to the rule of faith.

paras.t: Sive habentes ministerium ecclesiasticum, ut ordinati simus membra aliorum in ministrando eis sacramenta Ecclesiæ. Sive qui docet, id est gratiam instruendi habens, sit membrum alterius in doctrina, id est in exhibitione doctrinæ. Qui exhortatur, id est gratiam exhortationis sortitus, sit membrum aliorum in exhortando eos ad meliora. Qui tribuit eleemosynam, tribuat in simplicitate, id est simplici intentione, videlicet ad gloriam Dei, non propter laudem humanam. Qui præest, id est prælatus seu princeps, præsit sibi subjectis in sollicitudine, id est vigilanter et timorate, perpendens illud Sapientis : Judicium gravissimum in his qui præsunt, fiet. Si enim unumquemque nostrum, juxta Michæam prophetam, oporteat sollicite ambulare cum Deo suo, quanto magis aliorum prælatum, quem utique tanto sollicitum conversari oportet, quanto plurium animarum constitutus est custos? Qui miseretur, id est, aliis condolet et succurrit, in hilaritate cordis hoc faciat, ne suo mœrore miserum magis affligat. Unde de quibusdam scriptum est : Consolatores onerosi vos omnes. Quocontra ait Psalmista : Jucundus homo qui miseretur et commodat. Nec obest quod infra dicit Apostolus, Flere cum flentibus. Quamvis enim qui miseretur aliis, aliquo modo contristetur et lugeat, totum tamen fieri debet, non in dejectione spiritus, sed in hilaritate, quia ad hoc niti debet ut alterius miseriam relevet, eique animo læto subveniat.
paras.en: [[12:7|Or ministry|Sive habentes ministerium]]: if we have an ecclesiastical ministry, so that we are ordained as members of others [[12:7|in ministering|in ministrando]] the sacraments of the Church to them. [[12:7|or he that teacheth|Sive qui docet]], that is, one who has the grace of instructing, let him be a member of another [[12:7|in doctrine|in doctrina]], that is, in imparting teaching. [[12:8|He that exhorteth|Qui exhortatur]], that is, one who has been given the grace of exhortation, let him be a member of others [[12:8|in exhorting|in exhortando]] them to better things. [[12:8|he that giveth|Qui tribuit]] alms, let him give [[12:8|with simplicity|in simplicitate]], that is, with a single intention, namely for the glory of God, not for human praise. [[12:8|he that ruleth|Qui præest]], that is, a prelate or prince, let him rule those subject to him [[12:8|with carefulness|in sollicitudine]], that is, watchfully and with fear, weighing the words of the Wise Man: [[Wis 6:6|a most severe judgment shall be for them that bear rule|Judicium gravissimum in his qui præsunt, fiet]]. For if, according to the prophet Micheas, each of us must [[Mich 6:8|walk solicitous with thy God|sollicite ambulare cum Deo suo]], how much more the prelate of others, who must live the more carefully the more souls he has been made guardian of? [[12:8|he that sheweth mercy|Qui miseretur]], that is, who feels for others and helps them, let him do it [[12:8|with cheerfulness|in hilaritate]] of heart, lest by his own gloom he afflict the wretched man more. So it is written of some: [[Job 16:2|you are all troublesome comforters|Consolatores onerosi vos omnes]]. On the contrary the Psalmist says: [[Ps 111:5|Acceptable is the man that sheweth mercy and lendeth|Jucundus homo qui miseretur et commodat]] [*jucundus*, "acceptable" in the Douay-Rheims, also means "cheerful": the sense Denis wants here]. Nor does it stand in the way that the Apostle says below, [[Rom 12:15|weep with them that weep|Flere cum flentibus]]. For although he who has mercy on others is in some way saddened and mourns, still all must be done not in dejection of spirit but in cheerfulness, because he must strive to relieve the other's misery and come to his help with a glad mind.

paras.t: Dilectio Dei et proximi, sit sine simulatione, id est non ficta, quemadmodum scriptum est : Non diligamus verbo, neque lingua, sed opere et veritate. Simulatores autem et callidi provocant iram Dei. Simus quoque odientes malum culpæ in nobis ipsis et proximis; naturam vero et gratiam diligamus in omnibus; adhærentes bono, id est virtutibus, seu virtuosis hominibus, juxta illud : Cum viro sancto assiduus esto. Et iterum ait Scriptura : Quum videris sensatum, statim evigila ad illum. Caritatem fraternitatis invicem diligentes, id est, quod fratres se invicem diligant : ne sitis seminatores discordiæ, sed amantes communem caritatem in omnibus. Honore invicem prævenientes ex humilitate. Quilibet enim potest considerare aliquid boni in alio, quod ipse non habet; vel ex alia rationabili causa potest alteri primo reverentiam exhibere, vel intus in corde, vel foris. Exteriore autem honore invicem prævenire, maxime pertinet ad æquales, et subditos, ac juniores : et hoc utique multum nutrit caritatem fraternam. Propter quod Petrus : Omnes, inquit, honorate; et Christus in Evangelio, Qui major est vestrum, sit vester minister. Denique scriptum est : Quanto major es, humilia te in omnibus, et invenies gratiam coram Deo et hominibus. Aliqui vero sunt dura cervice, qui nec honorantes se sciunt rehonorare, nec superioribus suis debitam reverentiam exhibere. Ista honoratio proximi est actus duliæ, quæ est virtus debitam creaturis reverentiam afferens.
paras.en: [[12:9|Let love|Dilectio]] of God and neighbour be [[12:9|without dissimulation|sine simulatione]], that is, not feigned, as it is written: [[1 John 3:18|let us not love in word nor in tongue, but in deed and in truth|Non diligamus verbo, neque lingua, sed opere et veritate]]. [[Job 36:13|Dissemblers and crafty men prove the wrath of God|Simulatores autem et callidi provocant iram Dei]] [*provocant*, "provoke"]. Let us also be [[12:9|Hating that which is evil|odientes malum]] of guilt, in ourselves and in our neighbours, but let us love nature and grace in all; [[12:9|cleaving to that which is good|adhærentes bono]], that is, to the virtues, or to virtuous men, according to the words: [[Ecclus 37:15|be continually with a holy man|Cum viro sancto assiduus esto]]. And again Scripture says: [[Ecclus 6:36|if thou see a man of understanding, go to him early in the morning|Quum videris sensatum, statim evigila ad illum]] [the margin gives Prov. vi, 22; the words are those of Ecclus 6:36]. [[12:10|Loving one another with the charity of brotherhood|Caritatem fraternitatis invicem diligentes]], that is, that brothers love one another[[1 John 4:7||]][[1 John 4:12||]]: do not be sowers of discord, but lovers of common charity in all things[[1 Pet 4:8||]]. [[12:10|with honour preventing one another|Honore invicem prævenientes]] [preventing: going before, outdoing], out of humility. For anyone can consider some good in another that he himself has not; or for some other reasonable cause he can show reverence to another first, either inwardly in the heart or outwardly. To go before one another in outward honour belongs chiefly to equals, subjects and the young; and this greatly nourishes brotherly charity. For this reason Peter says: [[1 Pet 2:17|Honour all men|Omnes, inquit, honorate]]; and Christ in the Gospel: [[Matt 23:11|He that is the greatest among you shall be your servant|Qui major est vestrum, sit vester minister]]. Moreover it is written: [[Ecclus 3:20|The greater thou art, the more humble thyself in all things, and thou shalt find grace before God|Quanto major es, humilia te in omnibus, et invenies gratiam coram Deo]] and men. But some are stiff-necked, who know neither how to return honour to those who honour them nor how to show due reverence to their superiors. This honouring of one's neighbour is an act of dulia [the reverence due to creatures, as distinct from *latria*, the worship due to God alone], the virtue that shows creatures the reverence due to them.

paras.t: Sollicitudine non pigri ad habendam sollicitudinem bonam, quæ est vigilantia cordis in bonis; vel, Non pigri ad exsecutionem sollicitam veræ et intimæ sollicitudinis. Est autem quædam sollicitudo vana atque superflua, quæ versatur circa hæc temporalia, de qua Salomon ait: Exspectatio sollicitorum peribit; et Apostolus, Nihil (inquit) solliciti sitis. Spiritu ferventes calore divini amoris, ne caritas refrigescat in nobis, et evomat nos Christus. Domino servientes servitute latriæ, de qua scriptum est: Dominum Deum tuum timebis, et illi soli servies.
paras.en: [[12:11|In carefulness not slothful|Sollicitudine non pigri]] in having good carefulness, which is the watchfulness of the heart in good things; or, not slothful in carefully carrying out true and inward carefulness. For there is a vain and superfluous carefulness, which is busy about these temporal things, of which Solomon says: [[Prov 11:7|the expectation of the solicitous shall perish|Exspectatio sollicitorum peribit]]; and the Apostle: [[Phil 4:6|Be nothing solicitous|Nihil (inquit) solliciti sitis]]. [[12:11|In spirit fervent|Spiritu ferventes]] with the heat of divine love, lest charity grow cold in us[[Matt 24:12||]], and Christ vomit us out[[Apoc 3:16||]]. [[12:11|Serving the Lord|Domino servientes]] with the service of latria, of which it is written: [[Deut 6:13|Thou shalt fear the Lord thy God, and shalt serve him only|Dominum Deum tuum timebis, et illi soli servies]].

paras.t: Spe gaudentes, id est, de certa exspectatione futuræ beatitudinis spiritualiter jucundantes in Deo, qui vos ad æternam beatitudinem invitavit. Propter quod gratias referendum est ei indesinenter. Nihil enim Christiano felicius, cui promittuntur regna cœlorum. In tribulatione juste vel injuste illata, a mundo vel dæmone, estote patientes, repellendo a vobis passionem tristitiæ, quoniam scriptum est: Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam. Et alibi habetur: Illi qui tentationes non susceperunt in timore Dei et patientia, exterminati sunt. Denique omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo, persecutionem patientur; et per multas tribulationes oportet nos ingredi regnum cœlorum. Idcirco in tribulationibus, tanquam in optima via perveniendi ad Deum, oportet nos cordialiter exsultare. Ait enim Psalmista: Juxta est Dominus his qui tribulato sunt corde; et Dominus, Cum ipso (inquit) sum in tribulatione. Orationi instantes.
paras.en: [[12:12|Rejoicing in hope|Spe gaudentes]], that is, rejoicing spiritually in God in the sure expectation of the beatitude to come, God who has invited you to eternal beatitude. For this we must give Him thanks without ceasing. For nothing is happier than a Christian, to whom the kingdom of heaven is promised. [[12:12|in tribulation|In tribulatione]], whether brought on justly or unjustly, by the world or by the devil, be [[12:12|Patient|patientes]], driving away from you the passion of sadness, since it is written: [[Matt 5:10|Blessed are they that suffer persecution for justice' sake|Beati qui persecutionem patiuntur propter justitiam]]. And elsewhere we read: [[Jdt 8:24|But they that did not receive the trials with the fear of the Lord|Illi qui tentationes non susceperunt in timore Dei]] and patience, [[Jdt 8:25|Were destroyed|exterminati sunt]] [the margin gives Judith xiii, 24, 25; the words are those of Jdt 8:24–25]. Moreover, [[2 Tim 3:12|all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution|omnes qui volunt pie vivere in Christo, persecutionem patientur]]; and [[Acts 14:21|through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God|per multas tribulationes oportet nos ingredi regnum cœlorum]]. So in tribulations, as on the best way of coming to God, we must rejoice from the heart. For the Psalmist says: [[Ps 33:19|The Lord is nigh unto them that are of a contrite heart|Juxta est Dominus his qui tribulato sunt corde]]; and the Lord says: [[Ps 90:15|I am with him in tribulation|Cum ipso (inquit) sum in tribulatione]]. [[12:12|Instant in prayer|Orationi instantes]].

paras.t: Necessitatibus sanctorum, id est penuriis servorum Christi, estote communicantes, id est communia facientes bona vestra, supplendo eorum inopiam. Unde ad Hebræos dicit Apostolus: Beneficentiæ et communionis nolite oblivisci. Hospitalitatem sectantes, peregrinos et pauperes recipiendo gratis in propria domo: juxta illud, Egenos vagosque induc in domum tuam; item et illud, Hospitales invicem sine murmuratione. Hinc alibi dicit Apostolus: Hospitalitatem nolite oblivisci: per hanc enim placuerunt quidam, videlicet Abraham et Lot, angelis hospitio receptis. Joannes quoque in sua Canonica de quodam perverso conqueritur: Ipse non recipit fratres, et omnes qui recipiunt, prohibet. Ecce quantum amanda, sectanda et continuanda est Christianis virtus hospitalitatis, quæ tot Apostolorum testimoniis comprobatur. Nam et Christus in die judicii dicturus est reprobis: Hospes fui, et non collegistis me. Ideo ait beatus Job: Foris non remansit peregrinus, ostium meum viatori patuit.
paras.en: [[12:13|to the necessities of the saints|Necessitatibus sanctorum]], that is, to the wants of the servants of Christ, be [[12:13|Communicating|communicantes]], that is, making your goods common, supplying their need. So the Apostle says to the Hebrews: [[Heb 13:16|do not forget to do good and to impart|Beneficentiæ et communionis nolite oblivisci]]. [[12:13|Pursuing hospitality|Hospitalitatem sectantes]], taking pilgrims and the poor into your own house without charge: according to the words, [[Is 58:7|bring the needy and the harbourless into thy house|Egenos vagosque induc in domum tuam]]; and also, [[1 Pet 4:9|Using hospitality one towards another, without murmuring|Hospitales invicem sine murmuratione]]. Hence the Apostle says elsewhere: [[Heb 13:2|hospitality do not forget: for by this some|Hospitalitatem nolite oblivisci: per hanc enim placuerunt quidam]] were pleasing [Denis has *placuerunt*, "pleased", for the Vulgate's *latuerunt*, "being not aware of it"], namely Abraham and Lot[[Gen 18:3||]][[Gen 19:1||]], [[Heb 13:2|have entertained angels|angelis hospitio receptis]]. John too in his Canonical Epistle complains of a certain wicked man: [[3 John 1:10|neither doth he himself receive the brethren, and them that do receive them he forbiddeth|Ipse non recipit fratres, et omnes qui recipiunt, prohibet]]. See how much the virtue of hospitality is to be loved, pursued and kept up by Christians, being approved by the witness of so many Apostles. For Christ too will say to the reprobate on the day of judgment: [[Matt 25:43|I was a stranger and you took me not in|Hospes fui, et non collegistis me]]. So blessed Job says: [[Job 31:32|The stranger did not stay without, my door was open to the traveller|Foris non remansit peregrinus, ostium meum viatori patuit]].

paras.t: Benedicite, id est, bona dicite, et orate pro persequentibus vos; benedicite eis, et nolite maledicere eis. Repetitio, confirmationis et magnæ seriositatis indicium est. Hoc est quod ait Salvator: Orate pro persequentibus et calumniantibus vos; et, Benedicite maledicentibus vobis. Hoc faciendo, veraciter sequimur vestigia Christi, de quo Petrus affirmat: Quum malediceretur, non maledicebat; quum pateretur, non comminabatur.
paras.en: [[12:14|Bless|Benedicite]], that is, speak good, and pray, [[12:14|them that persecute you|pro persequentibus vos]]: [[12:14|bless|benedicite]] them, [[12:14|and curse not|et nolite maledicere]] them. The repetition is a sign of confirmation and of great earnestness. This is what the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:44|pray for them that persecute and calumniate you|Orate pro persequentibus et calumniantibus vos]]; and, [[Luke 6:28|Bless them that curse you|Benedicite maledicentibus vobis]]. Doing this, we truly follow in the footsteps of Christ, of whom Peter affirms: [[1 Pet 2:23|when he was reviled, did not revile: when he suffered, he threatened not|Quum malediceretur, non maledicebat; quum pateretur, non comminabatur]].

paras.t: Hortor insuper vos, Gaudere cum gaudentibus, id est congratulari his qui de bonis operibus gaudent in Domino. Non autem debemus cum perversis et vanis jucundis gaudere, de quibus scriptum est: Mundus gaudebit, vos autem contristabimini. Flere cum flentibus, condolendo afflictis, sicut Job ait: Flebam quondam super eo qui afflictus erat, et compatiebatur anima mea pauperi. Verumtamen non debemus cum omnibus flentibus æqualiter flere. Est enim fletus alius inordinatus, quo propter amissionem temporalium rerum quis superflue luget. Sic flentibus conflere debemus, compatiendo eorum errori, quatenus cessent sic flere. Alius est fletus ordinatus propter peccata, seu gloriæ dilationem. Sic flenti conflere debemus, quatenus veniam consequatur seu gloriam, non autem ut fletus talis statim tollatur ab eo, nisi forte per accidens obesset spiritui, inducendo corporis debilitatem aut aliud nocumentum. Imo simpliciter gaudendum est de bono fletu alterius.
paras.en: I urge you besides [[12:15|Rejoice with them that rejoice|Gaudere cum gaudentibus]], that is, to share the joy of those who rejoice in the Lord over good works. But we must not rejoice with the perverse and the vainly merry, of whom it is written: [[John 16:20|the world shall rejoice: and you shall be made sorrowful|Mundus gaudebit, vos autem contristabimini]]. [[12:15|weep with them that weep|Flere cum flentibus]], feeling for the afflicted, as Job says: [[Job 30:25|I wept heretofore for him that was afflicted, and my soul had compassion on the poor|Flebam quondam super eo qui afflictus erat, et compatiebatur anima mea pauperi]]. Yet we must not weep equally with all who weep. For one weeping is disordered, by which someone mourns excessively for the loss of temporal things. With those who weep so we must weep, pitying their error, so that they may cease to weep so. Another weeping is ordered, for sins, or for the delay of glory. With one who weeps so we must weep, that he may obtain pardon or glory, but not so that such weeping be taken from him at once, unless perhaps it should accidentally harm the spirit by bringing on bodily weakness or some other harm. Rather, one should simply rejoice at another's good weeping.

paras.t: Id ipsum invicem sentientes, id est, conformantes vos mutuo in affectu et in intellectu, ut sitis conformes in Domino. Non alta sapientes de vobismetipsis, id est, non magna præsumentes de vobis, sicut ait Psalmista : Domine, non est exaltatum cor meum, neque ambulavi in magnis; sed humilibus cogitationibus estote consentientes, ut parva et vilia æstimetis de vobis. Nolite esse prudentes apud vosmetipsos, id est in oculis propriis, reputando vos sapientes, aut ceteris magis sensatos. Imo si aliquid sapientiæ vel scientiæ in vobis est, totum Deo adscribite, et nolite in vobis ipsis inaniter exsultare, et simplices spernere. Unde Salomon dicit : Vidisti hominem sapientem sibi videri? magis illo spem stultus habebit. Et iterum : Prudentiæ tuæ pone modum. Et rursus alibi habetur : Væ qui sapientes estis in oculis vestris, et coram vobismetipsis prudentes.
paras.en: [[12:16|Being of one mind one towards another|Id ipsum invicem sentientes]], that is, conforming yourselves to one another in affection and understanding, so that you may be of like mind in the Lord. [[12:16|Not minding high things|Non alta sapientes]] of yourselves, that is, not presuming great things of yourselves, as the Psalmist says: [[Ps 130:1|Lord, my heart is not exalted|Domine, non est exaltatum cor meum]] … [[Ps 130:1|Neither have I walked in great matters|neque ambulavi in magnis]] [the margin's "Ps. xxx, 1" is cxxx, 1]; [[12:16|but consenting to the humble|sed humilibus cogitationibus estote consentientes]]: be of one accord with humble thoughts, so as to think small and lowly things of yourselves. [[12:16|Be not wise in your own conceits|Nolite esse prudentes apud vosmetipsos]], that is, in your own eyes, counting yourselves wise, or more sensible than others. Rather, if there is any wisdom or knowledge in you, ascribe it all to God, and do not exult vainly in yourselves and despise simple folk. So Solomon says: [[Prov 26:12|Hast thou seen a man wise in his own conceit? there shall be more hope of a fool than of him|Vidisti hominem sapientem sibi videri? magis illo spem stultus habebit]]. And again: [[Prov 23:4|set bounds to thy prudence|Prudentiæ tuæ pone modum]] [the margin gives Prov. xxvi, 4; the words are those of Prov 23:4]. And again elsewhere: [[Is 5:21|Woe to you that are wise in your own eyes, and prudent in your own conceits|Væ qui sapientes estis in oculis vestris, et coram vobismetipsis prudentes]].

paras.t: Nulli malum pro malo reddentes. Nam et Psalmista fatetur : Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala, decidam merito ab inimicis meis inanis. Sed nec hoc sufficit, quoniam Christus ait : Benefacite his qui oderunt vos; et Petrus : Non reddentes malum pro malo, sed econtrario benedicentes: in hoc enim vocati estis. Hæc impleri non valent, nisi privatus amor radicitus exstinguatur, et amor divinus mentem prorsus possideat. Providentes, id est, circumspecte seu provide disponentes ac operantes, bona, non tantum coram Deo, videlicet in secreto, vel quantum ad cordis intentionem, sed etiam coram omnibus hominibus, ne quis scandalizetur in vobis, salva tamen veritate vitæ, justitiæ et doctrinæ. Unde alibi dixit Apostolus : Honeste ambulemus ad eos qui foris sunt; et Salvator : Luceat lux […]
paras.en: [[12:17|To no man rendering evil for evil|Nulli malum pro malo reddentes]]. For the Psalmist too confesses: [[Ps 7:5|If I have rendered to them that repaid me evils, let me deservedly fall empty before my enemies|Si reddidi retribuentibus mihi mala, decidam merito ab inimicis meis inanis]] [the margin's "Ps. xxxiv, 5" does not fit; the words are those of Ps 7:5]. But not even this is enough, since Christ says: [[Matt 5:44|do good to them that hate you|Benefacite his qui oderunt vos]]; and Peter: [[1 Pet 3:9|Not rendering evil for evil|Non reddentes malum pro malo]], [[1 Pet 3:9|but contrariwise, blessing: for unto this are you called|sed econtrario benedicentes: in hoc enim vocati estis]]. These things cannot be fulfilled unless private love is rooted out and divine love wholly possesses the mind. [[12:17|Providing|Providentes]], that is, arranging and doing with circumspection or foresight, [[12:17|good things, not only in the sight of God|bona, non tantum coram Deo]], namely in secret, or as to the intention of the heart, [[12:17|but also in the sight of all men|sed etiam coram omnibus hominibus]], lest anyone be scandalized in you, saving always the truth of life, justice and teaching. So the Apostle said elsewhere: [[Rom 13:13|Let us walk honestly|Honeste ambulemus]] towards them that are without [these last words are from 1 Thess 4:11]; and the Saviour: [[Matt 5:16|let your light shine|Luceat lux]] […] [the rest of this column is lost in the transcription].

paras.t: Si fieri potest quod dicam, quod ex vobis est, id est, vestram possibilitatem facite ad hoc, ut sitis cum omnibus hominibus pacem veram ac spiritualem habentes, non carnalem et sæcularem de qua ait Salvator : Non veni pacem mittere. Non vosmetipsos defendentes, carissimi, repercutiendo percutientem, quum dicat Salvator : Si quis percusserit te in unam maxillam, præbe ei et alteram, scilicet quantum ad animi præparationem; sed date locum iræ, id est, vindictæ seu iracundiæ cedite, ne repercutiendo, alium magis provocetis, vel propriam passionem exerceatis. Scriptum est enim in Deuteronomio : Mihi vindictam committite, et ego retribuam, dicit Dominus, qui facio judicium omnibus injuriam patientibus. Nostra translatio talis est : Mea est ultio, et ego retribuam eis in tempore.
paras.en: [[12:18|If it be possible|Si fieri potest]], what I shall say, [[12:18|as much as is in you|quod ex vobis est]], that is, do all that is possible to you towards this, that you may [[12:18|have peace with all men|cum omnibus hominibus pacem habentes]], true and spiritual peace, not carnal and worldly peace, of which the Saviour says: [[Matt 10:34|I came not to send peace|Non veni pacem mittere]]. [[12:19|Revenge not yourselves, my dearly beloved|Non vosmetipsos defendentes, carissimi]], by striking back at him who strikes, since the Saviour says: [[Matt 5:39|if one strike thee on thy right cheek, turn to him also the other|Si quis percusserit te in unam maxillam, præbe ei et alteram]] [Denis: "on one cheek"], namely as regards the readiness of the mind; [[12:19|but give place unto wrath|sed date locum iræ]], that is, yield to vengeance or anger, lest by striking back you provoke the other more, or give rein to your own passion. [[12:19|for it is written|Scriptum est enim]] in Deuteronomy: [[12:19|Revenge is mine, I will repay, saith the Lord|Mihi vindictam committite, et ego retribuam, dicit Dominus]] [Denis reads "Leave vengeance to me"], who [[Ps 102:6|judgment for all that suffer wrong|judicium omnibus injuriam patientibus]][[Ps 145:7||]] [the margin gives Ps. cii, 6 and cxxv, 7, the second a misreading of cxlv, 7]. Our translation reads: [[Deut 32:35|Revenge is mine, and I will repay them in due time|Mea est ultio, et ego retribuam eis in tempore]].

paras.t: Sed si esurierit inimicus tuus qui te odit, ciba illum pane spirituali ac corporali, si potes; si sitit, potum da illi; et pari ratione, si veste eget, operi eum. Hoc enim faciens, carbones ignis, id est materiam dilectionis, congeres, id est, congregabis et pones, super caput, id est in mente ipsius. Hoc enim exstinguere potest rancorem et inflammare amorem. Hoc idem Salomon dicit in Proverbiis. Ex quo patet error Judæorum, dicentium quod secundum legis intentionem inimici sint odiendi, non solum quantum ad culpam, sed etiam quantum ad naturam. Sic enim non esset eis benefaciendum, sed malum faciendum. Contra quod scriptum est : Quum ceciderit inimicus tuus, ne gaudeas. Sanctus etiam Job ait : Si gavisus sum ad ruinam ejus qui me oderat, et exsultavi eo quod invenisset eum malum. Sed et Samuel deplanxit Saulem hostem suum letalem, usque ad diem mortis suæ.
paras.en: [[12:20|But if the enemy be hungry|Sed si esurierit inimicus tuus]], he who hates you, [[12:20|give him to eat|ciba illum]] with spiritual and bodily bread, if you can; [[12:20|if he thirst, give him to drink|si sitit, potum da illi]]; and by the same reasoning, if he needs clothing, clothe him. [[12:20|For, doing this, thou shalt heap coals of fire|hoc enim faciens, carbones ignis congeres]]: coals of fire, that is, the stuff of love; thou shalt heap, that is, gather and put, [[12:20|upon his head|super caput]], that is, in his mind. For this can quench rancour and kindle love. Solomon says the same in Proverbs[[Prov 25:21||]]. From this the error of the Jews is plain, who said that according to the intention of the law enemies were to be hated not only as to their guilt but also as to their nature. For then we should not do good to them but evil. Against this it is written: [[Prov 24:17|When thy enemy shall fall, be not glad|Quum ceciderit inimicus tuus, ne gaudeas]]. Holy Job too says: [[Job 31:29|If I have been glad at the downfall of him that hated me, and have rejoiced that evil had found him|Si gavisus sum ad ruinam ejus qui me oderat, et exsultavi eo quod invenisset eum malum]]. And Samuel too mourned for Saul, his deadly enemy, until the day of his death[[1 Kings 15:35||]].

paras.t: Noli vinci per impatientiam a malo, sed vince per fortitudinem animi in bono, id est tua bonitate, malum alterius, non apponendo malum malo, sed quo al[…]
paras.en: [[12:21|Be not overcome|Noli vinci]] through impatience [[12:21|by evil|a malo]], [[12:21|but overcome|sed vince]] by strength of mind [[12:21|by good|in bono]], that is, by your goodness, [[12:21|evil|malum]] of another, not adding evil to evil, but … […] [the end of the article is lost in the transcription].

13.title: Expositio capituli tertiidecimi: Omnis anima potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit.
13.title_en: Exposition of the thirteenth chapter: Let every soul be subject to higher powers.
13.note: In the commentary on verses 4–7 the transcription has kept only half of each line of one column; the gaps are marked and await a scan of the page.

paras.t: Erudivit Apostolus omnes fideles in moribus generaliter, capitulo præcedenti; jam specialiter instruit subditos, dicens: Omnis anima, id est omnis homo exsistens sub alio. A parte enim significat totum, sicut et in Actibus ait Lucas: Eramus autem universæ animæ in navi, ducentæ septuaginta sex. Potestatibus sublimioribus, id est in potestate constitutis, principibus sæcularibus, spiritualibusque prælatis, non solum bonis et modestis, sed etiam dyscolis, subdita sit per obedientiam promptam ac humilem, dummodo nihil præcipiant contra Deum et justitiam. Unde tyrannis obediendum non erat in his quibus impugnaverant fidem: et ministri qui eis placebant martyres persequendo, graviter peccaverunt; sicut et angeli inferiores, consentientes Lucifero. Non est enim potestas nisi a Deo omnipotente, a quo processit atque dependet omnis potestas creata ac limitata. Quamvis enim potestatis abusio seu nocendi voluntas sit ab animo creato, ipsa tamen potestas a Deo profluxit. Propter quod dixit Christus Pilato: Non haberes potestatem adversum me ullam, nisi tibi datum esset desuper. Et Sapiens dicit: Præbete aures, qui continetis multitudines, quoniam data est vobis potestas a Deo, et virtus ab Altissimo. Quæ autem a Deo sunt, ordinata sunt, id est sapienter et rationabiliter instituta. Omnia namque in mensura, numero et pondere constituit Deus. Denique, sapientia attingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponit universa suaviter. Ad sapientem enim pertinet ordinare.
paras.en: In the preceding chapter the Apostle instructed all the faithful in conduct in general; now he instructs subjects in particular, saying: [[13:1|Let every soul|Omnis anima]], that is, every man who stands under another. For he signifies the whole by a part, as Luke too says in the Acts: [[Acts 27:37|we were in all in the ship two hundred threescore and sixteen souls|Eramus autem universæ animæ in navi, ducentæ septuaginta sex]]. [[13:1|be subject to higher powers|potestatibus sublimioribus subdita sit]], that is, to those set in power, secular princes and spiritual prelates, not only the good and gentle but also [[1 Pet 2:18|the froward|dyscolis]], by ready and humble obedience, provided they command nothing against God and justice. Hence tyrants were not to be obeyed in the things in which they attacked the faith: and the servants who pleased them by persecuting the martyrs sinned gravely; as did the lower angels who consented to Lucifer. [[13:1|For there is no power but from God|Non est enim potestas nisi a Deo]], almighty, from whom all created and limited power has come forth and on whom it depends. For although the abuse of power, or the will to harm, is from the created mind, yet power itself flowed from God. For which reason Christ said to Pilate: [[John 19:11|Thou shouldst not have any power against me, unless it were given thee from above|Non haberes potestatem adversum me ullam, nisi tibi datum esset desuper]]. And the Wise man says: [[Wis 6:3|Give ear, you that rule the people|Præbete aures, qui continetis multitudines]] … [[Wis 6:4|For power is given you by the Lord, and strength by the most High|quoniam data est vobis potestas a Deo, et virtus ab Altissimo]]. [[13:1|and those that are ordained of God|Quæ autem a Deo sunt, ordinata sunt]], that is, established wisely and reasonably. For God has set all things [[Wis 11:21|in measure, and number, and weight|in mensura, numero et pondere]]. Moreover, wisdom [[Wis 8:1|reacheth, therefore, from end to end mightily, and ordereth all things sweetly|attingit a fine usque ad finem fortiter, et disponit universa suaviter]]. For it belongs to the wise man to order.

paras.t: Itaque qui resistit potestati per rebellionem, Dei ordinationi, id est rei a Deo ordinatæ, seu juri divino, vel etiam Deo, resistit, quantum in se est. Unde Deus dixit ad Samuelem: Non te abjecerunt, sed me. Et Christus: Qui vos spernit, me spernit. Moyses quoque ad filios Israel: Non contra nos, inquit, est murmur vestrum, sed contra Deum. Qui autem resistunt, ipsi sibi damnationem æternam acquirunt, peccando mortaliter. Interdum etiam incurrunt damnum temporale.
paras.en: [[13:2|Therefore, he that resisteth the power|Itaque qui resistit potestati]], by rebellion, [[13:2|resisteth the ordinance of God|Dei ordinationi resistit]], that is, the thing ordained by God, or the divine law, or even God himself, as far as lies in him. Hence God said to Samuel: [[1 Kings 8:7|they have not rejected thee, but me|Non te abjecerunt, sed me]]. And Christ: [[Luke 10:16|he that despiseth you despiseth me|Qui vos spernit, me spernit]]. Moses too to the children of Israel: [[Ex 16:8|your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord|Non contra nos, inquit, est murmur vestrum, sed contra Deum]], he says. [[13:2|And they that resist purchase to themselves damnation|Qui autem resistunt, ipsi sibi damnationem æternam acquirunt]], eternal damnation, by sinning mortally. Sometimes they also incur temporal loss.

paras.t: Deinde ostendit cur superioribus obediendum sit. Nam principes non sunt timori boni operis, id est ad timorem his qui bene agunt, sed mali, id est his qui agunt perverse. Officium enim et intentio principis est, subditos juste disponere, bonos ad meliora provehere, impios vero restringere et punire. Hoc tamen verum est de his qui potestate sibi concessa bene utuntur. Aliqui vero sunt principes mali, qui justos opprimunt et impios fovent. De quibus per Prophetam Dominus profitetur: Ipsi regnaverunt, et non ex me; principes exstiterunt, et non cognovi. Sed nec hi inordinate timendi sunt, quum dicat Salvator: Nolite timere eos qui corpus occidunt. Vis autem non timere, nec causam timendi habere potestatem, id est in potestate positum principem seu prælatum? Fac bonum, id est justitiam, et habebis laudem ex illa potestate, id est, a potestatem habente laudaberis, si bonus est. Si vero sit malus, habebis laudem ex eo occasionaliter, quoniam erit tibi causa majoris coronæ, laudis et gloriæ. Dei enim minister est prælatus seu princeps, etiamsi ignoret: nam divinæ dispositioni aliquo modo subservit; tibi in bonum, id est ad tuam utilitatem, quatenus retrahat te a malo, promoveatque ad bonum.
paras.en: Then he shows why superiors are to be obeyed. [[13:3|For princes are not a terror to the good work|Nam principes non sunt timori boni operis]], that is, a cause of fear to those who do well, [[13:3|but to the evil|sed mali]], that is, to those who act perversely. For the office and intention of a prince is to order his subjects justly, to advance the good to better things, and to restrain and punish the wicked. This, however, is true of those who use well the power granted them. But some princes are evil, who oppress the just and favour the wicked. Of whom the Lord declares through the Prophet: [[Osee 8:4|They have reigned, but not by me: they have been princes, and I knew not|Ipsi regnaverunt, et non ex me; principes exstiterunt, et non cognovi]]. But not even these are to be feared inordinately, since the Saviour says: [[Matt 10:28|fear ye not them that kill the body|Nolite timere eos qui corpus occidunt]]. [[13:3|Wilt thou then not be afraid of the power?|Vis autem non timere potestatem?]], and not have cause to fear, that is, the prince or prelate set in power? [[13:3|Do that which is good|Fac bonum]], that is, justice, [[13:3|and thou shalt have praise from the same|et habebis laudem ex illa]] power, that is, you will be praised by him who has power, if he is good. But if he is evil, you will have praise from him as an occasion, since he will be to you the cause of a greater crown, praise and glory. [[13:4|For he is God's minister|Dei enim minister est]], the prelate or prince, even if he does not know it: for he serves the divine disposition in some way; [[13:4|to thee, for good|tibi in bonum]], that is, for your profit, so that he may draw you back from evil and advance you to good.

paras.t: Si […] feceris, time potestatem tuæ perve[rsitatis] ultricem. […] portat. Potestas sæcularis portat […] um materialem; ecclesiastica, sp[iritua]lem. Utraque vero habet judiciariam potestatem, quæ per gladium designatur. Dei enim minister est princeps, […] in iram, id est in punitionem seu pœnam infligendam, ei qui malum agit […] est ratio qua gladium portat, ut […] mala, quatenus culpa ordinetur per pœnam. Ideoque necessitate, id est oblig[atione] juris, et propter vim coactivam su[perio]ris, videlicet, quia tenemini et p[otestis] ad hoc compelli, subditi estote sup[erioribus], non solum propter iram, id est […] pœnæ, sed etiam propter conscientiam mundam habendam, id est amore […], ne habeatis remorsum conscientiæ si invite obedieritis. Unde alio loco […] Apostolus: Non ad oculum servient[es …] sicut Domino. Ideo enim, scilicet a[d con]fitendum vestram subjectionem, et […] præstatis: quod est signum subjec[tionis]; ministri enim Dei sunt principes, […] sint exsecutores justitiæ divinæ. […] quod dicitur per Sapientem: Qu[um es]setis ministri regni ejus, etc. In […] sum servientes, id est, propter tribu[torum] receptionem ministrantes vobis, def[enden]do rem publicam, et pugnando pro […]. Reddite ergo, statim quum potest[is, om]nibus debita. Cui debetis tributum […] tributum; et cui debetis ve[ctigal,] reddite vectigal. Dicitur autem trib[utum] quod solvit tota patria pro se […] suo. Vectigal autem, quod solvit s[ingula]ris persona, ut quum negotiator […] vecturas et pedagia rerum suarum […] vectigal vocatur stipendium quod […] dominis, quando per terras vehuntur […] timorem debetis, videlicet domino […] no, ut cœlesti, exhibete timorem; […] betis honorem interiorem vel exte[riorem,] videlicet Deo, parentibus et virtuo[sis ho]minibus, date honorem. Ait enim D[ominus] per Prophetam: Filius honorat patrem, et servus timet dominum suum: si ergo pater ego sum, ubi est honor meus? et si dominus ego sum, ubi est timor meus?
paras.en: [in this part of the page the transcription has kept only the first half of each line of the right column; what remains is translated, and the gaps are marked] [[13:4|But if thou do that which is evil, fear|Si […] feceris, time]] the power that avenges your perversity. […] [[13:4|for he beareth not the sword in vain|portat]] […]. The secular power bears a material [sword]; the ecclesiastical, a spiritual one. Each has judicial power, which is signified by the sword. [[13:4|For he is God's minister|Dei enim minister est]], the prince, […] [[13:4|to execute wrath|in iram]], that is, to inflict punishment or penalty, [[13:4|upon him that doth evil|ei qui malum agit]] […] is the reason why he bears the sword, that […] evils, so that guilt may be ordered by punishment. [[13:5|Wherefore be subject of necessity|Ideoque necessitate, id est oblig[atione] juris, et propter vim coactivam su[perio]ris, videlicet, quia tenemini et p[otestis] ad hoc compelli, subditi estote]], *of necessity*, that is, by obligation of law, and because of the coercive force of the superior, namely because you are bound and can be compelled to it, be subject to superiors, [[13:5|not only for wrath|non solum propter iram]], that is, [for fear] of punishment, [[13:5|but also for conscience' sake|sed etiam propter conscientiam]], to keep it clean, that is, out of love […], lest you have remorse of conscience if you obey unwillingly. Hence in another place […] the Apostle: [[Col 3:22|not serving to the eye|Non ad oculum servientes]] […] [[Col 3:23|as to the Lord|sicut Domino]]. [[13:6|For therefore also you pay tribute|Ideo enim et præstatis]], namely to confess your subjection […]: which is a sign of subjection; [[13:6|For they are the ministers of God|ministri enim Dei sunt]], the princes, […] are executors of the divine justice. […] what is said through the Wise man: [[Wis 6:5|being ministers of his kingdom|Quum essetis ministri regni ejus]], etc. [[13:6|serving unto this purpose|In […] sum servientes]], that is, serving you for the receiving of tributes, defending the commonwealth and fighting for […]. [[13:7|Render therefore to all men their dues|Reddite ergo omnibus debita]][[Matt 22:21||]], at once, when you can. [[13:7|Tribute, to whom tribute is due|Cui debetis tributum […] tributum]] […]; [[13:7|custom, to whom custom|cui vectigal vectigal]], render custom. Tribute is what the whole country pays for itself […]. Custom is what a single person pays, as when a merchant […] the carriage and tolls of his goods […]; custom is also the name of the payment which […] to lords, when they are carried through their lands […] [[13:7|fear, to whom fear|timorem]] you owe, namely to the Lord […], as to the heavenly one, show fear; […] [[13:7|honour, to whom honour|honorem]], inward or outward, namely to God, to parents and to virtuous men, give honour. For the Lord says through the Prophet[[Mal 1:6||]]: [[Mal 1:6|The son honoureth the father, and the servant his master: if then I be a father, where is my honour? and if I be a master, where is my fear|Filius honorat patrem, et servus timet dominum suum: si ergo pater ego sum, ubi est honor meus? et si dominus ego sum, ubi est timor meus?]]

paras.t: Nemini quidquam debeatis, nisi ut invicem diligatis, quia dilectio, quotiescumque alteri impendatur, permanet jugiter in præcepto. Per dilectionem vero intelliguntur alii actus virtuosi quos unus tenetur alteri. Qui enim diligit proximum, legem implevit. Ratio quippe diligendi proximum, est Deus. Ergo qui proximum diligit, Deum diligit. Qui autem diligit Deum, implet mandata Decalogi scripta in prima tabula, quæ ordinantur ad caritatem divinam. Et qui diligit proximum, implet mandata Decalogi scripta in tabula secunda, quæ ordinantur ad caritatem fraternam. Ergo qui diligit proximum, legem implevit, præsertim quoad præcepta moralia. Quod declarat Apostolus:
paras.en: [[13:8|Owe no man any thing, but to love one another|Nemini quidquam debeatis, nisi ut invicem diligatis]], since love, however often it is bestowed on another, remains always under the precept. By love are understood the other virtuous acts that one owes another. [[13:8|For he that loveth his neighbour hath fulfilled the law|Qui enim diligit proximum, legem implevit]]. For the reason for loving one's neighbour is God. So he who loves his neighbour loves God. And he who loves God fulfils the commandments of the Decalogue written on the first table, which are ordered to the love of God. And he who loves his neighbour fulfils the commandments of the Decalogue written on the second table, which are ordered to brotherly love. So he who loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law, especially as to the moral precepts. Which the Apostle makes plain:

paras.t: Nam, non adulterabis, non occides, non furaberis, non falsum testimonium dices, non concupisces rem proximi tui: id est, præceptum de vitandis adulterio, homicidio, furto, falso testimonio, concupiscentia rei alienæ, et si quod, id est aliquod, aliud est mandatum inclusum vel reducendum ad ista, in hoc verbo instauratur, id est, comprehenditur atque impletur, videlicet: Diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum. Qui enim sic diligit proximum, sic facit ei quomodo vult fieri sibimetipsi: quum diligere nihil aliud sit nisi alicui bonum velle. Voluntas autem procedit in opus, si potest: si tamen fuerit vera et perfecta voluntas. Ideo subditur: Dilectio proximi malum non operatur: quia nec habens eam peccat mortaliter, nec proximo nocet, quamdiu eam habuerit. Plenitudo ergo, id est consummatio, perfecta impletio ac finalis perfectio, legis antiquæ et novæ, est dilectio Dei et proximi: quoniam omnium virtutum regina, origo, motrix ac finis est caritas, qua Deus amatur et proximus. Omnia ergo præcepta disponuntur et referuntur ad […] plenam observationem præcepti caritatis. Propter quod alibi habetur: Finis præcepti est caritas de corde puro, et conscientia bona, et fide non ficta. Hoc autem pensandum, quod licet sint duo præcepta caritatis, in quibus tota lex pendet et Prophetæ, unum tamen frequenter ponitur pro utroque, quia nec Deus sine proximo, nec proximus sine Deo diligitur. Hinc enim Salvator ait: Hoc est præceptum meum, ut diligatis invicem sicut dilexi vos. Et iterum dicit: Mandatum novum do vobis, ut diligatis invicem. De eo quoque scriptum est: Hæc est annuntiatio quam audistis ab initio, ut diligatis alterutrum.
paras.en: [[13:9|For: Thou shalt not commit adultery: Thou shalt not kill: Thou shalt not steal: Thou shalt not bear false witness: Thou shalt not covet|Nam, non adulterabis, non occides, non furaberis, non falsum testimonium dices, non concupisces]][[Ex 20:13||]][[Matt 19:18||]] your neighbour's goods: that is, the precept of avoiding adultery, murder, theft, false witness and coveting another's goods, [[13:9|And if there be any other commandment, it is comprised in this word|et si quod est aliud mandatum, in hoc verbo instauratur]], *if there be any*, that is, some, other commandment included in these or to be brought back to them, *it is comprised*, that is, contained and fulfilled, in this word, namely: [[13:9|Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself|Diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum]][[Lev 19:18||]][[Mark 12:31||]]. For he who so loves his neighbour does to him as he would have done to himself: since to love is nothing else than to will good to someone. And the will goes forth into deed if it can, provided it is a true and perfect will. Therefore there follows: [[13:10|The love of our neighbour worketh no evil|Dilectio proximi malum non operatur]]: since he who has it neither sins mortally nor harms his neighbour as long as he has it. [[13:10|Love therefore is the fulfilling of the law|Plenitudo ergo legis est dilectio]], *the fulfilling*, that is, the consummation, perfect fulfilment and final perfection, of the old and the new law, *is love* of God and neighbour: since charity, by which God and neighbour are loved, is the queen, origin, mover and end of all the virtues. All the precepts, then, are disposed and referred to […] the full keeping of the precept of charity. For which reason it is said elsewhere: [[1 Tim 1:5|Now the end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith|Finis præcepti est caritas de corde puro, et conscientia bona, et fide non ficta]]. It must be weighed that although there are two precepts of charity, [[Matt 22:40|On these two commandments dependeth the whole law and the prophets|in quibus tota lex pendet et Prophetæ]], yet one is often put for both, since neither is God loved without our neighbour, nor our neighbour without God. Hence the Saviour says: [[John 15:12|This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you|Hoc est præceptum meum, ut diligatis invicem sicut dilexi vos]]. And again he says: [[John 13:34|A new commandment I give unto you: That you love one another|Mandatum novum do vobis, ut diligatis invicem]]. Of it too it is written: [[1 John 3:11|this is the declaration which you have heard from the beginning, that you should love one another|Hæc est annuntiatio quam audistis ab initio, ut diligatis alterutrum]].

paras.t: Deinceps declarat Apostolus, quod actibus caritatis maxime insistendum sit tempore evangelicæ legis, quæ est lex caritatis ac libertatis, quemadmodum vetus lex erat lex timoris ac servitutis, prout prolixe manifestatum est supra. Ait ergo: Et hoc scientes tempus, id est, conditionem et opportunitatem considerantes præsentis temporis, quod est tempus gratiæ: de quo scriptum est, Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis; quia hora est jam, scilicet tempore isto, imo omni momento, nos de somno surgere, id est de torpore et negligentia ad opera caritatis procedere, atque ad vigilantiam mentis ascendere: sicut alibi clamat Apostolus, Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis. Otium autem, torpor et negligentia, somno comparantur, quoniam sicut somnus vitam naturæ abscondit, sic ista vitam gratiæ perimunt. Ad quod spiritualiter pertinet illud Jonæ: Quid tu sopore deprimeris? Surge et invoca Deum tuum. Denique non dormientibus, sed vigilantibus, provenit regnum Dei. Consequenter ponit rationem cur tempus est a somno surgere. Nunc enim, quum caritatem et gratiam Dei habemus, propior, id est vicinior, est nobis nostra salus, id est vita æterna, quam quum credidimus, id est, quam tunc quum solam fidem habuimus: quoniam fides sine operibus non unit nos Deo, nec perducit ad vitam æternam. Vel, Quam quum credidimus, id est, quam ante Christi adventum, quia tunc omnes sancti descenderunt ad limbum inferni. Nunc vero patefacta est nobis per Christum janua felicitatis æternæ: cui tanto amplius approximamus, quanto eam ardentius desideramus. Ambulamus enim ad eam, contemplando, amando et bene agendo.
paras.en: Next the Apostle makes plain that we must above all press on with acts of charity in the time of the law of the Gospel, which is the law of charity and freedom, as the old law was the law of fear and servitude, as was shown at length above[[Rom 8:15||]]. So he says: [[13:11|And that, knowing the season|Et hoc scientes tempus]], that is, considering the condition and opportunity of the present time, which is the time of grace: of which it is written, [[2 Cor 6:2|Behold, now is the acceptable time: behold, now is the day of salvation|Ecce nunc tempus acceptabile, ecce nunc dies salutis]]; [[13:11|that it is now the hour for us to rise from sleep|quia hora est jam, nos de somno surgere]], *now*, namely at this time, nay at every moment, that is, to go forward from torpor and negligence to the works of charity, and to rise up to watchfulness of mind: as the Apostle cries elsewhere: [[Eph 5:14|Rise, thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead|Surge, qui dormis, et exsurge a mortuis]]. Idleness, torpor and negligence are likened to sleep, since as sleep hides the life of nature, so these destroy the life of grace. To which belongs spiritually that word in Jonas: [[Jon 1:6|Why art thou fast asleep? rise up call upon thy God|Quid tu sopore deprimeris? Surge et invoca Deum tuum]]. Lastly, the kingdom of God comes not to those who sleep but to those who watch. Next he gives the reason why it is time to rise from sleep. [[13:11|For now our salvation is nearer|Nunc enim propior est nobis salus]], now that we have the charity and grace of God, *nearer*, that is, closer, *is our salvation*, that is, eternal life, [[13:11|than when we believed|quam quum credidimus]], that is, than then, when we had faith alone: since faith without works[[Jas 2:14||]] does not unite us to God nor lead us to eternal life. Or, *than when we believed*, that is, than before Christ's coming, since then all the saints went down to the limbo of hell. But now the gate of eternal happiness has been opened to us through Christ: to which we draw the nearer the more ardently we desire it. For we walk toward it by contemplating, loving and doing good.

paras.t: Nox, id est tempus infidelitatis et vitiorum, vel tempus veteris Testamenti, quod dicitur nox, propter obscuritatem legalium figurarum et prophetalium visionum: quæ omnia in nova lege revelantur. Unde dicitur ad Hebræos: Umbram habens lex futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum. Hæc igitur nox præcessit, id est præteriit, et modo non est; dies autem, id est claritas evangelicæ veritatis, splendor gratiæ, tempus novi Testamenti, seu beatitudo promissa, appropinquavit, quia jam præsens est in re, vel in spe. Gratia namque et veritas per Jesum Christum facta est. Abjiciamus ergo opera tenebrarum, id est peccata, quæ ex tenebris ignorantiæ prodeunt, mentem deformant, et ad tenebras inferi protrahunt. Omnis enim qui male agit, odit lucem, et non venit ad lucem, ut non arguantur opera ejus. Et induamur spiritualiter arma lucis, id est virtutes et dona Spiritus Sancti, quæ animam roborant et defendunt contra insidias dæmonum, et contra jacula seu prælia vitiorum. De quibus armis dicit alio loco: Accipite armaturam Dei, ut possitis resistere in die malo, induti loricam justitiæ, sumentes scutum fidei, et galeam salutis.
paras.en: [[13:12|The night|Nox]], that is, the time of unbelief and vices, or the time of the Old Testament, which is called night because of the obscurity of the figures of the law and of the visions of the prophets: all of which are revealed in the new law. Hence it is said to the Hebrews: [[Heb 10:1|having a shadow of the good things to come, not the very image of the things|Umbram habens lex futurorum bonorum, non ipsam imaginem rerum]]. This night, then, [[13:12|is passed|præcessit]], that is, has gone by and is no more; [[13:12|And the day|dies autem]], that is, the brightness of the truth of the Gospel, the splendour of grace, the time of the New Testament, or the promised beatitude, [[13:12|is at hand|appropinquavit]], since it is already present in reality, or in hope. For [[John 1:17|grace and truth came by Jesus Christ|Gratia namque et veritas per Jesum Christum facta est]]. [[13:12|Let us, therefore cast off the works of darkness|Abjiciamus ergo opera tenebrarum]], that is, sins, which come from the darkness of ignorance, disfigure the mind and drag it to the darkness of hell. For [[John 3:20|every one that doth evil hateth the light and cometh not to the light, that his works may not be reproved|Omnis enim qui male agit, odit lucem, et non venit ad lucem, ut non arguantur opera ejus]]. [[13:12|and put on the armour of light|Et induamur spiritualiter arma lucis]], spiritually, that is, the virtues and gifts of the Holy Ghost, which strengthen and defend the soul against the snares of the demons and against the darts or assaults of the vices. Of which armour he says in another place: [[Eph 6:13|take unto you the armour of God, that you may be able to resist in the evil day|Accipite armaturam Dei, ut possitis resistere in die malo]], [[Eph 6:14|having on the breastplate of justice|induti loricam justitiæ]], [[Eph 6:16|taking the shield of faith|sumentes scutum fidei]], [[Eph 6:17|the helmet of salvation|et galeam salutis]].

paras.t: Hæc ergo agamus sic, ut die, id est, quatenus tempore gratiæ, scilicet tempore isto, honeste ambulemus, id est, reverenter coram Deo, et exemplariter coram hominibus, conversemur, nemini dantes ullam offensionem, ut non vituperetur ministerium nostrum. Non in comessationibus et ebrietatibus, id est frequentibus, gulosis atque superfluis manducationibus et potationibus, fugiendo videlicet vitia gulæ, quæ valde inhonesta sunt. Propter quod ait Salvator: Videte ne graventur corda vestra crapula vel ebrietate: et Isaias, Væ qui consurgitis mane ad ebrietatem sectandam, et potandum usque ad vesperum. Non in cubilibus, id est voluptatibus carnis, quæ exercentur in cubiculis. Unde scriptum est: Væ qui dormitis in lectis eburneis, et lascivitis in stratis vestris. Et impudicitiis, id est ceteris luxuriæ vitiis, quæ sunt maxime impudica et bestialia, juxta illud: Fornicatio et ebrietas auferunt cor. Non in contentione, id est lite, et æmulatione, id est invidia. Scriptum est enim: Ubi zelus et contentio, ibi inconstantia et omne opus pravum. Et alibi Apostolus: Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio, nonne carnales estis?
paras.en: Let us do these things, then, [[13:13|Let us walk honestly, as in the day|sic, ut die, honeste ambulemus]], *as in the day*, that is, in the time of grace, namely at this time; *walk honestly*, that is, let us live reverently before God and as an example before men, [[2 Cor 6:3|Giving no offence to any man, that our ministry be not blamed|nemini dantes ullam offensionem, ut non vituperetur ministerium nostrum]]. [[13:13|not in rioting and drunkenness|Non in comessationibus et ebrietatibus]], that is, frequent, greedy and superfluous eating and drinking, fleeing namely the vices of gluttony, which are most unseemly. For which reason the Saviour says: [[Luke 21:34|take heed to yourselves, lest perhaps your hearts be overcharged with surfeiting and drunkenness|Videte ne graventur corda vestra crapula vel ebrietate]]; and Isaias: [[Is 5:11|Woe to you that rise up early in the morning to follow drunkenness, and to drink in the evening|Væ qui consurgitis mane ad ebrietatem sectandam, et potandum usque ad vesperum]]. [[13:13|not in chambering|Non in cubilibus]], that is, the pleasures of the flesh, which are practised in bedchambers. Hence it is written: [[Amos 6:4|You that sleep upon beds of ivory, and are wanton on your couches|qui dormitis in lectis eburneis, et lascivitis in stratis vestris]] [Denis begins "Woe to you", from the verse before]. [[13:13|and impurities|Et impudicitiis]], that is, the other vices of lust, which are most shameless and bestial, according to that word: [[Osee 4:11|Fornication, and wine, and drunkenness, take away the understanding|Fornicatio et ebrietas auferunt cor]] [Denis: "fornication and drunkenness take away the heart"]. [[13:13|not in contention|Non in contentione]], that is, strife, [[13:13|and envy|et æmulatione]], that is, envy. For it is written: [[Jas 3:16|where envying and contention is: there is inconstancy and every evil work|Ubi zelus et contentio, ibi inconstantia et omne opus pravum]]. And elsewhere the Apostle: [[1 Cor 3:3|whereas there is among you envying and contention, are you not carnal|Quum sit inter vos zelus et contentio, nonne carnales estis?]] [the line ends in this column are cut in the transcription and have been restored by sense]

paras.t: Sed induimini Dominum Jesum Christum, id est, brachiis sanctæ dilectionis complectimini eum in cordibus vestris, dicentes cum Sponsa: Tenui illum, nec dimittam. Vel, Induimini Dominum Jesum, id est, formam conversationis ejus sequimini, ut ipse per caritatem commoretur in vobis, ornet ac vestiat vos. Et carnis curam, id est provisionem victus et vestitus, quibus caro sustentatur, ne feceritis in desideriis superfluis, id est secundum concupiscentiam carnis, sed quantum necessitas exigit, et ratio dictat, quemadmodum alibi legitur: Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus. Unde Salomon: Mendicitatem et divitias ne dederis mihi, tribue tantum victui meo necessaria. Quid enim prodest moriturum hanc carnem, cito futuram vermium escam, delicate nutrire, et nobilem immortalemque animam, summæ Trinitatis imagine insignitam, negligere?
paras.en: [[13:14|But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ|Sed induimini Dominum Jesum Christum]], that is, embrace him in your hearts with the arms of holy love, saying with the Bride: [[Cant 3:4|I held him: and I will not let him go|Tenui illum, nec dimittam]]. Or, *put ye on the Lord Jesus*, that is, follow the pattern of his way of life, so that he may dwell in you through charity, and adorn and clothe you. [[13:14|and make not provision for the flesh|et carnis curam ne feceritis]], that is, provision of food and clothing by which the flesh is kept up, [[13:14|in its concupiscences|in desideriis]], superfluous ones, that is, according to the concupiscence of the flesh, but as far as necessity requires and reason dictates, as is read elsewhere: [[1 Tim 6:8|But having food and wherewith to be covered, with these we are content|Habentes victum et quibus tegamur, his contenti simus]]. Hence Solomon: [[Prov 30:8|Give me neither beggary, nor riches: give me only the necessaries of life|Mendicitatem et divitias ne dederis mihi, tribue tantum victui meo necessaria]]. For what does it profit to nourish delicately this flesh, which is to die and will soon be food for worms, and to neglect the noble and immortal soul, marked with the image of the most high Trinity? [the end of this article stands on the first page of Art. XVIII in the transcription]

14.title: Expositio capituli quartidecimi: Infirmum autem in fide assumite
14.title_en: Explanation of the fourteenth chapter: Now him that is weak in faith, take unto you
14.note: Some lines are lost in the transcription in v. 2, at the page break in v. 9, in v. 11 and in v. 20.

paras.t: Manifestavit Apostolus in superiori capitulo, quomodo inferiores ad superiores se debeant habere, jam docet quomodo superiores se habeant ad inferiores. Agnoscendum vero, quod in Ecclesia Romanorum, cui scribit Apostolus, erant quidam ex Judaismo conversi, qui erant legis æmulatores, cærimonialia legis observanda putantes : propter quod inter cibos discernebant secundum legis præcepta. Isti vocantur infirmi, id est imperfecti in fide catholica : quia secundum fidei veritatem, cærimonialia legis cessare cœperunt post Christi passionem, ut dictum est. Alii erant ex gentilitate conversi : et isti non discernebant in cibis humano usui deditis, prout ad Timotheum dicit Apostolus : Nihil rejiciendum quod cum gratiarum actione sumitur.
paras.en: In the chapter before, the Apostle showed how inferiors ought to behave towards superiors; now he teaches how superiors should behave towards inferiors. It must be understood that in the Church of the Romans, to which the Apostle writes, there were some converted from Judaism who were zealous for the law, thinking that the ceremonies of the law must be kept: and so they made distinctions between foods according to the precepts of the law. These are called weak, that is, imperfect in the Catholic faith: because, according to the truth of the faith, the ceremonies of the law began to cease after Christ's passion, as has been said. Others were converted from the Gentiles: and these made no distinction among foods given for man's use, as the Apostle says to Timothy: [[1 Tim 4:4|nothing to be rejected that is received with thanksgiving|Nihil rejiciendum quod cum gratiarum actione sumitur]] [the beginning of this article is damaged in the transcription, where the ends of the lines have been put in another place; it has been put back together from those pieces].

paras.t: Ait ergo : Infirmum autem, id est imperfecte edoctum, in fide, assumite, id est caritative instruite, et nolite ægrum abjicere, vos qui perfectiores estis in fide, exemplo Christi, qui ait : Venit Filius hominis quærere et salvum facere quod perierat. Talem ergo assumite, non in disceptationibus cogitationum, id est, non discutiendo seu judicando secreta cordis ejus, quæ soli Deo sunt cognita. Alius enim, ille scilicet qui novit cessasse legalia, credit, id est, fideliter noscit, […] manæ vitæ sustentationi apta, ita ut præceptum legis de discretione ciborum eum non obligat. Qui autem infirmus est in fide, ita non putans, sed inter cibos dis[…] per […] ad vitandum consentire scrupulum.
paras.en: So he says: [[14:1|Now him that is weak|Infirmum autem]], that is, imperfectly taught, [[14:1|in faith, take unto you|in fide, assumite]], that is, instruct him charitably, and do not cast off the sick man, you who are more perfect in faith, after the example of Christ, who says: [[Luke 19:10|the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost|Venit Filius hominis quærere et salvum facere quod perierat]]. Take such a one to you, then, [[14:1|not in disputes about thoughts|non in disceptationibus cogitationum]], that is, not by discussing or judging the secrets of his heart, which are known to God alone. [[14:2|For one believeth|Alius enim credit]], namely he who knows that the legal observances have ceased, believes, that is, faithfully knows, […] [the transcription loses some lines here: "that he may eat all things", that is, all foods] fit for the support of human life, so that the precept of the law on the distinction of foods does not bind him. [[14:2|but he that is weak|Qui autem infirmus est]] in faith, not thinking so, but making distinctions between foods, […] [more is lost here, with the words "let him eat herbs"] … to consent, so as to avoid a scruple.

paras.t: Notandum autem, quod legalia seu cærimonialia, quamvis statim post Christi passionem mortua erant, non tamen mortifera. Nam a tempore passionis usque ad Evangelii publicationem, poterant sine periculo observari, præcipue a Judæis conversis, dummodo non ponebatur spes salutis in eis, sed firmiter credebatur quod sine observatione eorum sufficere ad salutem fides et gratia Christi. Sic nempe in Actibus Apostolorum leguntur Apostoli ea servasse. Idcirco Apostolus dicit hunc infirmum in fide, non satis instructum de cessatione legalium, suo judicio relinquendum, donec melius informetur.
paras.en: Note, however, that the legal or ceremonial observances, though dead immediately after Christ's passion, were not yet deadly [dead but not deadly: after the Passion they no longer gave grace, but keeping them was not yet a mortal sin]. For from the time of the passion until the publishing of the Gospel they could be kept without danger, especially by converted Jews, provided that the hope of salvation was not placed in them, but it was firmly believed that the faith and grace of Christ were sufficient for salvation without keeping them. So indeed we read in the Acts of the Apostles that the Apostles kept them[[Acts 15:10||]][[Acts 16:3||]][[Acts 18:18||]][[Acts 21:26||]]. Therefore the Apostle says that this man who is weak in faith, not well enough instructed about the ceasing of the legal observances, is to be left to his own judgment until he is better informed.

paras.t: Is qui manducat indifferenter quemlibet cibum homini aptum, non manducantem hoc modo, sed inter cibos discernentem, non spernat tanquam iniquum, quum legalia nondum essent mortifera. Et qui non manducat, id est, iste inter cibos discernens et ab aliquibus abstinens, manducantem indifferenter non judicet tanquam legis transgressorem, quia lex cessavit quantum ad vim obligativam. Deus enim illum manducantem assumpsit ad fidem, sicut et non manducantem. De his itaque quæ bono animo fieri possunt et malo, non judicemus, sed potius in melius interpretemur.
paras.en: [[14:3|Let not him that eateth|Is qui manducat]] any food fit for man without distinction [[14:3|despise him that eateth not|non manducantem non spernat]] in this way, but makes distinctions between foods, as wicked, since the legal observances were not yet deadly. [[14:3|and he that eateth not|Et qui non manducat]], that is, he who distinguishes between foods and abstains from some, [[14:3|let him not judge him that eateth|manducantem indifferenter non judicet]] without distinction, as a transgressor of the law, because the law has ceased as to its binding force. [[14:3|For God hath taken him to him|Deus enim illum manducantem assumpsit]]: God has taken him who eats to the faith, as also him who does not eat. So in things that can be done with a good mind or a bad one, let us not judge, but rather take them in the better sense.

paras.t: Præterea probat Apostolus, quam irrationabile sit alium judicare inordinate. Tu quis es, id est cujus vel quantæ auctoritatis, qui judicas judicio reprobationis (judicium enim approbationis non est ita illicitum) alienum servum, id est proximum tuum, qui est servus Dei, et conservus tuus, super quem jurisdictionem non habes? Domino suo stat aut cadit, id est, ad gloriam vel irreverentiam Dei bene agit aut male, et ad eum pertinet judicare de hoc, non ad te. Stabit autem, id est, erectus erit corde ad Deum et bene aget. Hoc est verbum bonæ spei : tanquam diceret, Hoc pie præsumi potest, quod stabit, etiam si jam jacere videatur. Potens est enim Deus statuere, id est per gratiam a casu peccati erigere, illum. Per hoc ergo quod ait Apostolus, Stabit autem, duo docentur : primum, ut dubia trahamus in melius; secundum, ut nec impium simpliciter judicemus, quia nescimus qualis futurus sit. De hac autem materia, scilicet quomodo judicare sit licitum vel illicitum, plurima dicta sunt in expositione secundi capituli, quæ illic diffuse induxi, ne cogerer eadem sæpe repetere, sed semper ad illum locum lectorem remitterem.
paras.en: Further, the Apostle proves how unreasonable it is to judge another inordinately. [[14:4|Who art thou|Tu quis es]], that is, of whose or of how great authority are you, [[14:4|that judgest|qui judicas]] with a judgment of condemnation (for a judgment of approval is not so unlawful) [[14:4|another man's servant|alienum servum]], that is, your neighbour, who is the servant of God and your fellow servant, over whom you have no jurisdiction? [[14:4|To his own lord he standeth or falleth|Domino suo stat aut cadit]], that is, he does well or ill to the glory or the dishonour of God, and it belongs to Him to judge of this, not to you. [[14:4|And he shall stand|Stabit autem]], that is, he will be upright in heart towards God and will do well. This is a word of good hope: as if he said, this may piously be presumed, that he will stand, even if he now seems to lie fallen. [[14:4|for God is able to make him stand|potens est enim Deus statuere illum]], that is, to raise him up by grace from the fall of sin. By the Apostle's words, "and he shall stand," then, two things are taught: first, that we should take doubtful things in the better sense; second, that we should not judge even the wicked absolutely, because we do not know what he will become. On this matter, namely how judging is lawful or unlawful, much was said in the explanation of the second chapter[[Rom 2:1||]], which I set out at length there so as not to be forced to repeat the same things often, but always to send the reader back to that place.

paras.t: Adhuc ostendit Apostolus, vitandum esse judicium inordinatum. Nam alius judicat diem certum pro exercenda abstinentia eligendum : diem, inquam, interpositum inter diem alium, quo putat non esse abstinendum ; alius autem judicat omnem diem in abstinentia expendendum. Tanquam dicat : Unus putat certis diebus abstinendum, ut Pharisæus qui jejunabat bis in sabbato, seu in hebdomada. Alius judicat singulis diebus abstinendum, ut Judith, quæ jejunabat cunctis diebus, præter sabbata, neomenias et festa ; et sanctissima illa evangelica Anna de tribu Aser, quæ non discedebat de templo, die ac nocte serviens Domino in orationibus atque jejuniis. Quoniam vero utrumque horum bono animo fieri potest seu licite, ideo unus alium judicare non debet. Unde subjungitur : Unusquisque in suo sensu, id est in proprio intellectu, sententia seu consilio, abundet in bonum, id est, quilibet relinquatur suo judicio in hoc, permittaturque agere quod secundum suam conscientiam judicat melius esse, dummodo tamen non exeat limites rerum quæ licent.
paras.en: The Apostle shows further that inordinate judgment is to be avoided. [[14:5|For one judgeth between day and day|Nam alius judicat diem inter diem]]: one judges that a certain day is to be chosen for practising abstinence, a day, I say, set between another day, on which he thinks one should not abstain; [[14:5|and another judgeth every day|alius autem judicat omnem diem]] to be spent in abstinence. As if he said: one thinks one should abstain on certain days, like the Pharisee who fasted twice in the sabbath, that is, in the week[[Luke 18:12||]]. Another judges that one should abstain every day, like Judith, who fasted all the days except the sabbaths, new moons and feasts[[Jdt 8:6||]]; and that most holy Anna of the Gospel, of the tribe of Aser, who did not depart from the temple, serving the Lord day and night in prayers and fastings[[Luke 2:37||]]. Since either of these can be done with a good mind, that is, lawfully, one should not judge the other. So it is added: [[14:5|Let every man abound in his own sense|unusquisque in suo sensu abundet]], that is, in his own understanding, opinion or counsel, abound in good: that is, let each be left to his own judgment in this, and be allowed to do what he judges better according to his conscience, provided he does not go beyond the limits of what is lawful.

paras.t: Qui sapit diem, id est, certum diem, vel omnem diem discernit seu judicat abstinentiæ deputandum, Domino sapit, id est, ad gloriam Dei hoc agit, intendens Deo placere. Et qui manducat quemlibet cibum sine discretione legis, vel qui non jejunat quotidie, Domino manducat, id est, ad Dei honorem hoc facit, cujus dona manducat; gratias enim agit Deo omnium bonorum datori pro beneficiis suis. Et qui non manducat, scilicet quemcumque cibum, sed juxta legis tenorem inter cibos discernit, vel omni die jejunat, Domino non manducat, id est, ad gloriam Domini abstinet, et gratias agit Deo. Et ita uterque bene facit pro tempore, sicut ostensum est. Sic ergo agere debemus, omnia referendo ad Deum, ut glorificetur ipse in omnibus. Cujus ratio subditur :
paras.en: [[14:6|He that regardeth the day|Qui sapit diem]], that is, who discerns or judges a certain day, or every day, to be given to abstinence, [[14:6|regardeth it unto the Lord|Domino sapit]], that is, does it for the glory of God, intending to please God. [[14:6|And he that eateth|Et qui manducat]] any food without the distinction of the law, or who does not fast daily, [[14:6|eateth to the Lord|Domino manducat]], that is, does it for the honour of God, whose gifts he eats; [[14:6|for he giveth thanks to God|gratias enim agit Deo]], the giver of all good things, for His benefits. [[14:6|And he that eateth not|Et qui non manducat]], namely any food whatever, but distinguishes between foods according to the tenor of the law, or fasts every day, [[14:6|to the Lord he eateth not|Domino non manducat]], that is, abstains for the glory of the Lord, [[14:6|and giveth thanks to God|et gratias agit Deo]]. And so each does well for the time being, as has been shown. So we ought to act, referring all things to God, that He may be glorified in all. The reason for this is added:

paras.t: Nemo enim nostrum sibi vivit finaliter, id est ad gloriam propriam, quoniam vita naturæ et vita gratiæ quam habemus, ad gloriam et laudem Dei est ordinanda, tanquam ad ultimum finem. Et nemo nostrum sibi moritur, id est ad propriam laudem, sed ad gloriam Dei, quatenus separatus corpore, laudet atque glorificet Deum in patria indesinenter. Sive enim vivimus, Domino, id est ad gloriam Domini, vivimus; sive morimur, Domino morimur. Sive ergo vivimus, sive morimur, Domini sumus, id est, non solum jure creationis et gubernationis, sed per caritatem et cultum devotissimum, ad Dominum pertinemus. Beati qui ita conjuncti Deo sunt, ut tota vita morsque ipsorum Deum honoret. Ipse enim ait : Qui glorificaverit me, glorificabo eum. Omnia ergo opera nostra interiora et exteriora ad Dei gloriam referamus, et propter Deum omnia finaliter operemur.
paras.en: [[14:7|For none of us liveth to himself|Nemo enim nostrum sibi vivit]] as his end, that is, for his own glory, since the life of nature and the life of grace which we have are to be ordered to the glory and praise of God as to their last end. [[14:7|and no man dieth to himself|Et nemo nostrum sibi moritur]], that is, for his own praise, but for the glory of God, so that, separated from the body, he may praise and glorify God in the fatherland without ceasing. [[14:8|For whether we live, we live unto the Lord|Sive enim vivemus, Domino vivimus]], that is, for the glory of the Lord; [[14:8|or whether we die, we die unto the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or whether we die, we are the Lord's|sive morimur, Domino morimur. Sive ergo vivimus, sive morimur, Domini sumus]], that is, we belong to the Lord not only by right of creation and government, but by charity and most devout worship. Blessed are they who are so joined to God that their whole life and death honour God. For He Himself says: [[1 Kings 2:30|whosoever shall glorify me, him will I glorify|Qui glorificaverit me, glorificabo eum]]. Let us then refer all our works, inward and outward, to the glory of God, and do all things for God as our end.

paras.t: In hoc enim, id est propter hoc, Christus mortuus est et resurrexit, ut et vivorum et mortuorum dominetur, id est, dominari cognoscatur. Nam ante passionem erat utique vivorum mortuorumque Dominus, etiam secundum naturam assumptam ut Verbo unitam, quæ a primo instanti unionis suæ cum Verbo, prælata est omni creaturæ, dominiumque universale sortita. Propter quod ait Salvator : Pater diligit Filium, et omnia dedit in manu ejus ; et alibi, Dedisti ei potestatem omnis carnis. Verumtamen Christus dicitur passus ut omnium dominetur, propter duo : Primo, quoniam sua passione […] talem dominationem, non obstante quod ante habuerit ista. Non enim inconveniens est, idem alicui propter diversas causas competere. Secundo, quia post passionem cœpit ubique manifestari atque cognosci dominium Christi. Propter quod ait : Data est mihi omnis potestas in cœlo et in terra. Potest etiam ita exponi : Ut et vivorum et mortuorum dominetur, id est, spiritualiter vivos ac mortuos, scilicet justos et impios, in suo obsequio occupet. Unde ipse loquitur : Ego si exaltatus fuero a terra, omnia traham ad me ipsum.
paras.en: [[14:9|For to this end|In hoc enim]], that is, for this reason, [[14:9|Christ died and rose again: that he might be Lord both of the dead and of the living|Christus mortuus est et resurrexit, ut et vivorum et mortuorum dominetur]], that is, that He might be known to be Lord. For before the passion He was indeed Lord of the living and the dead, even according to the nature He assumed, as united to the Word, which from the first instant of its union with the Word was set above every creature and received universal dominion. For this reason the Saviour says: [[John 3:35|The Father loveth the Son: and he hath given all things into his hand|Pater diligit Filium, et omnia dedit in manu ejus]]; and elsewhere: [[John 17:2|thou hast given him power over all flesh|Dedisti ei potestatem omnis carnis]]. Yet Christ is said to have suffered that He might be Lord of all, for two reasons.
